Sub-standard Foreign Consumer Articles 
*341. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news- item 
published in the Times of India dated the 30* April, 2001 under the caption, "India 
witnesses the food, bad and ugly of foreign goods invasion"; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken to check the sub-standard foreign 
consumable wh :ch have Hooded the Indian market since the removal of 
quantitative restrictions? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHANTA KUMAR): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) Overall, import in dollar value have not registered an increase after 
removal of quantitative restrictions; in fact they have marginally declined during 
the period April-June, 2001 , compared to the corresp onding period in the year 
2000. Government have taken various measures to ensure that imported edibles and 
food products conform to the requirements of Indian laws such as me Prevention of 
Food Adulteration Act, 1954, and Rules made thereunder, Fruit Products Order, 
1955, Meat Food Products Order, 1973, the Standards of Weights and Measures 
(Packaged Commodities) Rules, 1977. The re quirements of these laws have been 
specifically made applicable to imported goods through notifications issued by 
Government in the Department of Commerce under the Foreign Trade 
(Development and Regulation) Act, 1992. Instructions have been issued to customs 
authorities to clear imports of goods including edibles and food products only after 
checking that they comply with the requirements of Indian laws. 
Sensitization training programmes were oryanized by the Ministry of Health 
and Family Weliare (Directorate General of-Health Services) at Delhi, Mumbai, 
Kolkata,

It also called for the freezing of funds and other financial resources, inluding

Therefore came the UN Security Coun cil Resolution 1333, which became 
Chapter VII Resolution, and, as th e hon. Member knows, Chapter VII 
Resolutions are enforceable not only on the country to which they refer, but on 
member States or member-countries of the United nations. This permits the UN 
Security Council to take enforcement measures. This Resolution requires the 
Taliban to (a) cease the provision of sa nctuary and training for international 
terrorists and to ensure that the territory under their control is not used for 
terrorist installations and camps; (b) hand over Osama Bin Laden; and (c) halt all

World Conference against Racism and Xenophobia 
*348. SHRI RAJU PARMAR: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) who is going to represent Government side at the World Conference against 
racism and xenophobia to be held at Durban; 
(b) how many non-official representatives would be sent to the Conference; 
(c) whether it is a fact that a number of individuals and organisations belonging to 
Dalit Communities have requested Government to allow, discussion regarding 
discrimination on the basis of castes in India; and 
(d) if so, what action is proposed in the matter? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (d) 
The composition of the delegation to represent India at the World Conference Against 
Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance, scheduled to be held 
in Durban, South Africa from August 31st—September 7th, 2001 is being finalised. 
A National Committee had been set up by the Prime Minister on December 16, 
2000, under the Chairm anship of the Minister of Ex ternal Affairs to aid India's 
participation in the World Conference. This Committee has assisted in ensuring that a 
wider nationwide discussion and preparation be enabled; also that India's participation 
in the conference is meaningful, constructive and in consonance with our national 
policies. 
The National Committee has, so far, held two sessions—in New Delhi in February 
2001 and at Hyderabad in June 2001. At its Hyderabad session, the Committee heard 
presentations by around fifty NGOs. We ar e inspireu and guided by the legacy of 
Mahatma Gandhi, Dr. Ambedkar and other social reformers on issues relating to caste 
discrimination. Several NGOs expressed the view that while there were constitutional 
and legal safeguards against discrimination on the basis of caste, and that whereas 
Government had initiated affirmative action programmes, discrimination continues to 
exist at the social level. 
The National Committee has deliberated on th ese presentations and other relevant 
material, too. It has concluded that while there was need to strengthen the national 
structures and institutions to ensure a more effective implementation of the constitutional 
and legislative provisions, also our affirmative action programmes, this was not a matter for 
any international initiative or intervention. They have, therefore, advised that it would 
not be appropriate to include this issu e on the Agenda of the Conference. The 
Government intends to act accordingly.

reported by the State Governments. During the year 1999-2000 and 2000-2001 as many as 8195 
and 5256 bonded labourers have been released and rehabilitated respectively. In the current 
financial year (2000-2001) up to 30th June 2001, as many as 3844 bonded labourers have been

Wheat supplied to Iraq 
† 2586. SHRI RAMA SHANKER KAUSHIK: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether wheat was to be supplied from India to Iraq, if so, the quantity thereof and the 
quantity of wheat which has been already supplied to Iraq so far; 
(b) whether Iraq has rejected the wheat, if so, the reasons therefor and the quantity thereof; 
and 
(c) in what manner Government would utilise the wheat which has been sent back and 
whether any financial loss has been incurred in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS. FOOD 
AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIRAM CHAUHAN): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. A 
quantity of 3.5 lakh MTs of wheat was contracted with the Grain Board of Iraq. Iraq has 
rejected to total quantity of 74.018 MT shipped. Quality specifications prescribed in the 
Iraqi contract provided for the presence of foreign matter upto 2%. There was no further 
break-up of this 2% into organic and inorganic foreign matter. As per the International 
CODEX standards, foreign matter in the grain is permissible upto 2% out of which 1.5% 
consists of reorganic matter, such as, chaff, weed seeds, other edible and non-edible grains, 
etc. and the balance (0.5%) inorganic foreign matter, such as, stones, dust etc. The Iraqi 
authorities however, do not count sand, stones, pebbles, clay particles etc. under foreign 
matter. The exporters did not know this position. The presumed that, as in the CODEX 
standards, the 2% foreign matter would include 0.5% in organic matter. Iraqi flour mills do 
not have adequate facilities for separation of inorganic matter because of the problem of 
spare parts required for maintenance of such machines owing to UN sanctions. 
(c) The consignments were reportedly diverted by the exporters to other destinations in Middle 
East where the buyers accepted the same. No financial loss has been incurred by the 
Government.

AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the newsreport captioned 
"sting off consumer law" as appeared in the Telegraph' dated 5th July, 2001; 
(b) if so. Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) what measures are proposed to be taken in this regard; and 
(d) whether Government would revise the amendments proposed in the Consumer 
Protection Act to make it effective and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, 
FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. SREENIVASA PRASAD): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The proposed amendment of section 3 of the Consumer Protection Act 
1986, to exclude claims in re spect of which corresponding remedies of judicial nature 
are available under any special law, for the time being in force, is intended to bring 
clarity and prevent conflict of jurisdiction with other statutes while at the same time 
ensuring that redressal is available to the consumer for complaints against defective 
goods or deficient services. 
An enabling provision for the payment along with the complaint of such amount of 
fee-as may be prescribed in the Rules, ha s been included in the proposed amendments 
to the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 essentia lly to discourage the filing of frivolous 
complaints and also to cover part of the expenses on service of notice, etc. 
(d) Amendments to the Consumer Protection Act. 1986 have been proposed after the 
deliberation and discussion with all concerned to make the Act more effective and purposeful.

FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Planning Commission has shown its dissatisfaction 
with the present Public Distribution System where the subsidy amount in the preceding 
year was around Rs. 12,500 crores; 
(b) if so, whether the State Governments are not very enthusiastic about this scheme 
as shown by poor off-take by the States and even poorer actual lifting by the Below 
Poverty Line families; 
 
(c) in view of the above whether any modi fied Public Distribution System is 
proposed to be launched whereby active co-operation of the State Government would 
be ensured; and 
(d) if so, what are the details thereof? 
56 

[16 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, 
FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIRAM CHAUHAN): (a) to 
(d) Planning Commission in its mid term appraisal of the 9th Five Year Plan has 
made some recommendations on PDS. The recommendations, inter alia, state that the 
coverage of TPDS and food subsidy should be restricted to the population below 
poverty line, items other than rice and wheat need to be excluded from TPDS, sugar 
supply through PDS draws well-to-do families to the system and ration cards have 
tended to be used as identity cards to establish people's identity which should be 
discouraged. 
The introduction of TPDS in June 1997 with its focus on the poor was a step in 
this direction. From 1.4.2000 the subsidy on foodgrains for APL families was 
eliminated while availability of foodgrains was ensured for them. However, in 
view of excess stocks in Central Pool, a discount of 30% of the economic cost has 
been given for APL families w.e.f. 12.7.2001. With effect from 1.4.2000 the BPL 
quota of foodgrains was doubled from lOKg. to 20 Kg. per family per month at 50% 
of economic cost. Though after this increase in the prices of the BPL foodgrains the 
offtake of wheat and rice has not increased in proportion to doubling of the 
allocations, there has been an overall increase in the offtake. 
With regard to levy sugar, the allocation under PDS has been restricted to only 
BPL families except in case of NE Region, island territories and hill States w.e.f. 
1.2.2001. State Govemments/UT Administrations have been advised to discourage 
the use of ration cards as documents of identity and to allow its use only for 
drawing PDS items.

Issue Prices of foodgrains meant for distribution to the families living below poverty 
line have been kept at levels which are lower than the market prices to ensure higher 
offtake. The offtake for BPL families has been about 80% of the allotment during 
1999-2000. The offtake of foodgrains under BPL category has been about 66.3% of the 
allotment during 2000-2001. The allotment for BPL families was increased from 10 
kg. to 20 kg. off foodgrains per family per month at 50% of economic cost from 1.4.2000. 
Although the increase in offtake during 2000-2001 has not been proportionate to the 
'doubling' of allocation made during the y ear, there has been an  overall increase in 
offtake under this category during 2000-2001 as compared to 1999-2000. So, it is not 
correct to say that there has been no offtake of foodgrains resulting in starvation like 
conditions in the States. Besides, PDS is supplemental in nature and does not meet the 
full requirement of a family belonging to any section of the population.

2647. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) as a flawed and discriminated treaty and that

(b) if so, what are the details of the position in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI 
OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Government's position on this issue is contained in External Affairs Minister's 
suo motu statement in Paliament on 9 May 2000. A copy is enclosed as Statement. 
Statement 
SUO MOTU Statement by the Minister of External Affairs on the NPT review 
conference 
The sixth Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) Review Conference is currently 
taking place in New York. Consistent with  our policy India is not attending the 
Conference. 
2. Since independence India has been a strong proponent of global nuclear 
disarmament and has taken numerous initiatives towards this objective. We remain 
committed to nuclear non-proliferation. In dia holds that genuine and lasting non- 
proliferation can only be achieved through  agreements that are based upon equality 
and non-discrimation, for only these can contribute to global peace and stability. 
3. In 1995, the NPT was extended indefinitely and unconditionally. Hontole Members 
would be aware that 187 countries are today parties to the NPT The proponents of 
NPT cite these developments as evidence of NPTs success; yet, it is also clear that 
there exist strong differences even among the NPT States Parties. Three of the five 
86 

[16 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Review Conferences held so far failed to reach any agreement on a 'final 
document'. The non-nuclear weapon States  Parties to the NPT have increasingly 
felt let down by the lack of progress on disarmament, as well as non-compliance 
with the basic provisions of the Treaty. 
4. The nuclear weapon States Parties to  the NPT and their allies have not 
diminished the role of nuclear weapons in  their respective or collective security 
calculus; on the contrary, new doctrines a nd justifications have been developed. 
NATO's new strategic concept, announced last year, ten years after the end of the 
Cold War, goes to re-emphasising a need for the continued retention of nuclear 
weapons. The nuclear weapons sharing arrangements within NATO also pose serious 
questions about compliance. Such developments are clear and continuing violations 
of the provisions of the NPT. This the NPT community has been unable to discuss, 
let alone deal with. 
5. One of the basic obligations of the nuclear-weapon-states under the NPT was 
to prevent further proliferation. The record  on this has also not been satisfactory. 
The nuclear-weapon-states have either b een active collaborators in or silent 
spectators to continuing proliferation, including exports of nuclear weapon related 
components and technologies. 
 
6. After more than three decades, the nuclear weapon States Parties to the NPT 
remain to be persuaded to begin any kind of collective, meaningful negotiations 
aimed at global nuclear disarmament. Thes e countries were expected to display a 
special responsibility to implement Article VI; instead, this special responsibility 
today appears to be arrogated as a perm anent special right to possess nuclear 
weapons and only for their exclusive security. 
7. India is a nuclear weapon state. Thou gh not a party to the NPT, India's 
policies have been consistent with the key provisions of NPT that apply to nuclear 
weapon states. These provisions are contained in Articles I, HI and VI. Article I 
obliges a nuclear weapon state not to transfer nuclear weapons to any other country 
or assist any other country to acquire them and India's record on non-proliferation 
has been impeccable. Article III requires a party to the Treaty to provide nuclear 
material and related equipment to any other country only under safeguards; India's 
exports of such materials have always been under safeguards. Article VI commits 
the parties to pursue negotiations to bring about eventual global nuclear 
disarmament. It needs to be emphasised that India today is the only nuclear 
weapon state that remains committed to  commencing negotiations for a Nuclear 
Weapons Convention, in order to bring about a nuclear-weapon-free-world, the 
very objective envisaged in Article VI of the NPT. 
8. After the tests undertaken by India in May, 1998, we have declared that India 
shall only maintain a minumum credible deterrent and not engage in any arms race. 
The role of India's nuclear weapons is defensive; accordingly, India has announced 
a 
87 

RAJYA SABHA [ 16 August, 2001 ] 
policy of no-first-use and a policy of non-use against non-nuclear weapon states. In 
fact, this meets the demand of unqualified negative security assurances, raised by the 
large majority of non-nuclear weapon states  to ensure their security. India has also 
indicated readiness to provide requisite assu rances to the nuclear-weapon-free-zones in 
existence or those being negotiated. We have also taken new initiative calling for 
dealerting of nuclear weapons as a means of reducing the risk of accidental or 
unauthorised launch. 
9. The NPT community needs to  understand that India cannot join the NPT as a 
non-nuclear weapon state. Statements by NPT States Parties about India rolling back its 
nuclear programme are mere diversions to prevent focussed attention on the basic goals 
of the NPT. 
10.India's commitment to global nuclear disarmament and lasting non-proliferation 
remains undiluted. While willing to co mmence negotiations on Nuclear Weapons 
Convention, India also remains ready to participate in agreed and irreversible steps to 
prepare the ground for such negotiations. A global no-first-use agreement and a non-use 
agreement against non-nuclear weapon states would meet the longstanding requirement 
for legally binding negative security assura nces and assurances to nuclear-weapon-free 
zones. Another positive development would be a commitment by nuclear weapon states 
not to deploy nuclear weapons outside their own national territories. Nuclear weapon 
states also need to take steps to lower the alert status, through gradual de-alerting 
actions, consistent with policies of rio-first-use and the defensive role of nuclear 
weapons. Tactical weapons th at lend themselves to war fighting roles need to be 
eliminated. These would be some positive and concrete steps in the right direction. 
11. India has been a responsible member of the international nuclear non- 
proliferation regime and will continue to  take initiatives and work with like-minded 
countries to bring about stable, genuine and la sting non-proliferation, thus leading to a 
nuclear-weapon-free- world.

2654. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be

them have been living there for generations. Many of them do not possess Nepali 
Citizenship Certificate as a result of which they do not enjoy facilities like land 
ownership, employment etc. in Nepal. There are, however, no reports of discrimination

300,000 as reported by the Hindustan Times) of the 34,090 citizenship certificates issued

Nepal as invalid. These citizenship certificates issued to applicants in 20 Districts of the 
Nepal terai belt were declared null ami void on grounds of procedural deficiencies. Mr.

one month, to all those people whose c itizenship papers were revoked by the 
Supreme Court citing procedural mistakes while issuing them. The problem of 
state-less terai Nepalese is a complex and sensitive issue in Nepal and has 
remained unresolved for a long time. An attempt to get an amendment 
incorporated into the Nepal Citizenship Act of 1964 through a Finance Bill 
earlier this year by the Government of former Prime Minister G P Koirala also 
failed as the Supreme Court declared it to be unconstitutional. Some political 
parties of Nepal have been advocating that it can be resolved only through an 
amendment to the Constitution which can be achieved only through discussions 
and political consensus within Nepal.

Downsizing of Government 
2694. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a draft approach paper prepared in connection with the 
Tenth Five Year Plan has recommended drastic downsizing of Government 
establishment in order to trimdown the bloated bureaucracy; 
(b) if so, the details of the suggestions made; 
(c) the Government's response thereto; and 
(d) by when a decision is likely to be taken to implement the recommendations? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE 
REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES OF THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (d) In the 
course of the mid-term appraisal of the Ninth Five Year Plan and formulation of the 
Approach Paper for the Tenth Five Year Plan, Planning Commission has made certain 
suggestions regarding reforms in governance practices and downsizing with a view to 
reshaping the bureaucracy and improving its effectiveness in discharging its functions. 
The Draft Approach Paper to the Tenth Five Year Plan is yet to be approved by the 
National Development Council. It is, however, seen that the suggestions with respect 
to downsizing referred to above include identification of surplus staff, setting up an 
effective re-deployment plan and a liberal system for exit. There is also reference to 
control on recruitment to various vacant posts of secretarial and clerical nature etc. 
The Central Government has taken steps in the recent past with a view to rights ize 
the government manpower. In 1992, the Government had decided to reduce the number of 
posts at various levels by 10% and, as a result, nearly 1.83 lakh posts have been 
abolished. An Expenditure Reforms Commission has been set up, inter alia, to review 
the road map for reducing the functions, activities and administrative structure of the 
Central Government. The Commission has submitted seven Reports so far and these 
reports have been forwarded to the concerned Ministries/Departments for 
implementation. In pursuance of the Finance Minister's announcement in his Budget 
Speech in the Parliament on 28 February, 2001 regarding limiting the fresh recruitment, the 
Department of Personnel and Training have issued instructions in May, 2001 requesting 
all the Ministries/Departments of the Government of India to restrict the recruitment to 
one-third of the direct recruitment vacancies occurring in each year subject to further 
ceiling that this does not exceed 1% of the total sanctioned strength of 
Ministries/Departments. The Ministries/Departments have accordingly been advised to 
prepare the Annual Direct Recruitment Plans, starting with the anticipated vacancies in the 
current financial year.

Priority to refonru and performance 
2703. SHRI K..M. SAIFULLAH: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government propose to give priority to "Reforms and 
Performance" for Normal Central Assistance (NCA) to States; and

more weightage given to development of infrastructure sector and social 
infrastructure for the 10th Plan. 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
ARUN SHOURIE): (a) Allocation of Normal Central Assistance (NCA) for 
Annual Plans of States is based on the Gadgil Formula as approved by the National 
Development Council (NDC) in December 1991. Any change in the 
priority/weightage of the Formula requires the approval of the NDC. However, 
since the Stales have sought a revision of the Formula, Planning Commission 
has sought their views and suggestions have been received from various State 
Governments. However, there is vide divergence in the-views amongst the 
States in this regard. In general, while the advanced States have sought higher 
weightage for performance, the less advanced States have sought higher 
weightage for backwardness. Hence, the Full Planning Commission in its 
meeting held on 27the & 29th June, 2001 discussed, inter-alia, the issue of revision 
of Gadgil Formula and in view of the divergence of the views among the State 
Governments and the sensitivity of this issue, it was decided that it would be 
necessary to discuss this further and evol ve a consensus before alternatives are 
considered by the NDC.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) Under MPLADS. 
works recommended by the Members of Parliament are to be implemented by the District 
Heads by' following the established procedur e of the concerned State Governments. To 
ensure that the implementation does not suffer for want of funds, it has been decided to 
release funds, under the Scheme, on the basis of cost of works sanctioned. The next 
instalment of Rs. 1 crore is released when the unsanctioned balance in respect of a Lok 
Sabha Constituency or a Rajya Sabha MP falls below Rs. 50 lakhs. 
(b) to (d) The percentage utilisation over release has been less than 70% since 
inception of the Scheme. The sanctions are normally issued by the concerned District Heads 
after receipt of funds. The utilisation occurs thereafter. There is, thus, always a time lag 
between the release of funds and its actual expenditure. Factors tike civil nature of works

DR. BIPLAB DASGUPTA : Sir, before coming here, I was in England 
and there the people are discussing only about recession. There is recession 
impending because things have slowed down in the U.S. It was a question of 
time before the recession is going to end. This was the discussion going on 
over there. The debate was on, when t he recession was going to end, whether 
before the end of the month or the end of the year. Some people were saying 
that the recession had already set in England, and they were in the middle of it. 
I could see a lot of seriousness in the way the debate was going on in 
England. Everybody was conc erned over there and felt that nothing much can 
be done about it. Everybody attributed it to the loss of market in the U.S. 
Globalisation was an important factor wh ich they attributed as a cause for the 
recession. That is important. 
When I come here, this debate and discussion is going on. It seems 
that there is a certain amount of indi fference, as if nothing can be done about 
the recession, as if something has been ordained by fate, it could not be 
touched by human action and you must acc ept that it has come. That is the 
kind of attitude I have seen in the Government. There is no sense of urgency 
that something very serious is going to happen. This is something inevitable, is 
the kind of an attitude I see in the Go vernment which is really depressing for 
me. Now, the recession is because of gl obalisation, because of its link with the 
Western World. The more the globalisat ion, the more the recession. That is 
more or less the position we find ourselves in today. If you compare the years 
of globalisation, the decade of the Nineties with the preceding decade of 
Eighties when there was no globalisation,  one can see certain features coming 
out by a simple comparison of the Eighties with the Nineties. If you look at the 
Economic Survey, as my friend, Narendra Mohan has told me, we find, for 
example, we have done very badly in agri culture. Between the Eighties and the 
Nineties, we had done much better in t he Eighties than the Nineties. This is 
number one. As far as industry is .concerned; if you look at all these figures and 
take the lean year average for all the y ears of the Nineties and compare   with 
lean year average for all the years of   the Eighties, we find 
     192 

[ 16 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
that the GDP was something around 8.5 per cent while in the Nineties it was 
much less than that. We find that we have done badly in agriculture, we have 
done badly in industry, including two basic industries, the basic activities. Still 
we find that our GDP growth has been more than 6 per cent. How is it when 
there is no growth in the agriculture, when there is no growth in the industry 
and when growth in steel is negligible? The solution lies in the service sector. 
Services, as we all know, is a catch-a ll sector. Services is something which 
explains everything and includes everyt hing. There is also a problem with 
regard to statistics how vthey are worked out and maintained. Statistics are 
maintained in one way in Western countries but in another way in our 
country. So, it is difficult to say. But the point is we need to discuss very 
seriously whether the estimates of our national income made according to 
these figures are right or not. Agriculture has gone down, the industry has 
gone down. How can it be that the GD P has gone up? It cannot be. Now, we 
can make the services go up by raising salaries. That itself will be reflected in 
the GDP growth. So there are certain statistical problems and I do not want 
to go into them. But without going into the problem if we only think that some 
GDP growth has taken place, that is not  material and that will not satisfy us. 
On the whole, in the Eighties, we had done better- than the Nineties. In other 
words, this globalisation has not benefited us very much. Now, the ultimate 
goal of globalisation is capital account  convertibility. When the currency is 
convertible in the capital account, that is ultimate in globalisation, but then 
the whole thing is not under your contro l. It is in the control of the super 
States. As Narendra Mohanji was asking why can't we have 5 per cent 
interest. We can have, if there is fa ir globalisation. It means that our 
borrowing rate should also be less than five per cent. You can lend at five per 
cent if you are borrowing at less than fi ve per cent. If the borrowing rate is 
three per cent, you can lend it at five per cent. But if the borrowing rate 
remains at three per cent or four per cent, nobody would lend you any 
money. But in this case if we accept the logic of capital account convertibility, 
then let this be done. I remember Dr. Manmohan Singh, from the very 
beginning when he introduced these reforms, had been consistently talking 
about capital account convertibility. He used to say when he was a Minister, 
that it would be within six months or  one year and he used to announce in 
conferences, in parties, etc., that we  would be going through the process of 
capital account convertibility. We opposed it. We said in Parliament that it 
would be wrong. Even those who were supposed to be supporters of 
globalisation said that this should be the very last step.   It is 
193 

RAJYA SABHA           [ 16 August, 2001 ] 
very dangerous and very risky. Very few countries have done it. A very few 
countries have done it in the Third World. When the East Asian crisis took 
place and when the issue came up for discussion in Parliament, our 
Government took a lot of credit that we have avoided the crisis here. How? 
By not going through the capital account convertibility. But that is not because 
of the Government. The Government wanted to go for it. Some credit should 
also come to us because we had opposed that there should not be any 
capital account convertibility. 
A point has been raised about the SEBI. I see all kinds of things 
being said in this House about the rate of growth. There was, at some stage, 
some trouble. The rate of growth was about 9 per cent, then 8 per cent and 
then 7 per cent. The essential thing is t hat whatever you wish, you can get it. 
Whatever you want, you get it. But that is not possible. There is a 
methodology behind it. There is some technology behind it. There is some 
way of doing behind it. If you want an incremental capital ratio of 4:1, then, to 
achieve a growth of 7 per cent, you require a savings rate pf 28 per cent. In 
our case, the savings rate is somethi ng like 22 per cent or 23 per cent. But 
the required rate is 28 per cent. Now, unless you increase the savings to the 
level of the East Asian countries, it is very difficult. The East Asian countries 
have a stupendous level of savings. They have got around 35 per cent or 40 
per cent or even 50 per cent of savings. Sir, Singapore has got a savings rate 
of something like 50 per cent. So, unless you achieve that higher rate of 
savings, you cannot have a higher rate of investment, you cannot have a 
higher rate of GDP. That is a very simp le economics. But I see, that is also 
lacking, from the point of view of the thinking of the Government. Unless you 
raise the level of savings, you cannot raise the GDP. Now, the East Asian 
countries went in for higher savings. Now, higher savings had been achieved 
- I am not talking about the last part of the crisis stage because of 
globalisation, but before that -when they  were actually developing. The East 
Asian countries developed because of  the banks and not because of the 
investment in share market. Almost all the savings was done by the banks, 
and the banks come under the public sector. It was the public-owned banks 
which have accumulated so much of savings. In our country, we go in for 
share market. And there are scams of one sort or the other, like US-64 and 
other things. The result is: The middle class is demoralised and they do not 
want to invest in the share market. Bu t, in the East Asian countries, the high 
savings rate had been achieved by simply making use of the banking system, 
which is under the public ownership.   Why you emphasis so much on share 
market, I do

not understand. The East Asian countries avoided the share market. I think, they 
all know about the pitfalls of the share market. But, still, they achieved a very 
high rate of growth with a very high in terest savings. Why can't our own banks 
have a very high interest savings, I do not understand. 
Then, we come to another aspect of globalisation. It is the opening up of 
the market and removal of the Quantitat ive Restrictions. Si r, the Quantitative 
Restrictions are no longer there. No w, anybody can send his things to any 
market. It is the meaning of globalisation. This is how we are devaluing. Now, 
what is the reason for going in for glo balisation in such a big way? When we 
started learning economics, one of the things which were taught to us was, 
"Infant industry argument." Which means, every country has the right to set up 
its own industry, and when an industry is se t up, for some time, it has a right to 
put quantitative restrictions. It is part of the universal logic that you impose 
quantitative restrictions and keep the fo reign companies out, allow the private 
companies to grow for a certain period of time, and then you remove the 
restrictions, if you want. If you want, you can review the Quantitative Restrictions 
on all the items, which, I think, is very dangerous. Now, the Government is 
saying that it has not affected us very much because there has been no surge in 
imports. There might not be any immediat e surge in import s. This will not 
happen immediately. It takes time. Moreover, the surge in imports is not very 
good. But the point is, specifically for the products which are affected, I get all 
kinds of letters from the victims of this po licy. They write to us, to me, to others, 
about the problems that the domestic i ndustries are facing because of the 
removal of Quantitative Restrictions. I w ill not go beyond this point because one 
more speaker is there from bur side. He will also speak. So, I think these issues 
should be very much in your mind and should be stressed when you go to Doha. 
These issues, should certainly be taken into account and discussed with other 
parties which can collaborate with us to form a united front.   Thank you very 
much.

SHRI SURYABHAN PATIL VAHADANE: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
refer to answer to Unstarred Question 705, given in the Rajya Sabha on 27th

(a) the details of the shortcomings found by the Group constituted by

THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. 
MURLIMANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) The shortcomings found in the functioning of the Institution of 
Mechanical Engineers (India), Mumbai by the Group constituted by the High 
Level Committee are given in statement I (See below). 
† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Anil 
Sharma. 
                                                                   1

RAJYA SABHA [ 17 August, 2001] 
(b) The date of effect of the tempor ary suspension of the examinations 
being conducted by the Institution of Mechanical Engineers (India), Mumbai 
came into effect from 23.5.2001, the date of issue of notification. 
(c) The recognition is granted on case to case basis by the High Level 
Committee after examining the comments offered by the All India Council for 
Technical Education. If required the opinion of expert groups formed by the 
High Level Committee is also obtained. Recognition of qualifications are subject 
to review by the High Level Committee. 
Statement-I 
Shortcomings found by the Group formed by the High Level Committee 
are as follows: 
(i) The Institution of Mechanical Engineers (India), Mumbai i.e. IME 
is being operated in an ad-hoc manner. No records of all activities 
are maintained. 
(ii) The management of IME is not along accepted norms. 
(iii) The IME could not provide documents to convince the Committee 
that curriculum meetings were held at regular intervals and that 
the revision of curriculum ever took place. 
(iv) IME appears to be reluctant to give full details of the names, 
qualifications and affiliations of all examiners. It appears that these 
appointments are done in an ad-hoc fashion. There are no 
Committee meeting minutes to suppor t the appointments. In fact ' 
IME has itself stated that they have  no records of qualifications of 
Examiners. Records sh ow that some individuals have been 
examiners/paper-setters for severa l (twenty plus) diverse subjects. 
Like-wise some individuals have examined hundreds of projects. 
Some examiners do not appear to be degree holders in Mechanical 
Engineering. 
(v) Coaching classes are closely asso ciated with IME—this is plain 
from the fact that Governing Council has gone on record to thank 
them. There is no evidence of any contact programmes. 
(vi) A few individuals have extensively travelled abroad on IME 
funds—incurring excessive expenses for short visits. There are no 
records on the outcome/benefits of these visits. 
2 

[ 17 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(vii) The Governing Council and the corporate members have over the 
years not shown any concern about the affairs of IME—despite 
being aware that Ministry of Human Resource Development had 
withdrawn its recognition of IME exams 20 years age. Ministry of 
Human Resource Development perhaps restored recognition a year 
later upon a promise by IME to reform its systems but this does not 
seem to have happened. 
(viii) Wim a very poor passing percentage IME seems to have benefited 
a miniscule percentage (around 1 %) of registered candidates and 
most of the others have contributed their valuable earnings to the 
huge cash reserves and assets of IME.

Funds to States under National Agriculture Insurance Scheme 
*363. SHRI GANDHI AZAD: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the State Governments are implementing New agriculture 
Policy-2000; and 
(b) if so, how many States have availed of funds on account of National 
Agriculture Insurance Scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) and (b)A Statement is laid on the Table of 
the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) The first ever National Agriculture Policy was announed in July, 2000. 
Various Central Sector and Centrally Sponsored Schemes are being implemented 
by the Government of India and the State Governments for development of 
agriculture and allied activities as envisaged in the Agriculture Policy. Several 
major initiatives have been taken in th e recent past to accelerate the pace of 
development and implement the objectives of the National Agriculture Policy, 
such as introduction of the Macro Management Scheme, preparation of common 
guidelines for Watershed Development Programmes, creation of Watershed 
Development Fund with a corpus of Rs. 200 crore, launching of a Technology 
Mission for the Integrated Development of Horticulture in North Eastern States, 
introduction of a Scheme for seed crop  insurance, establishment of a Seed 
Bank, measures for increasing the availability of farm credit, introduction of a 
subsidy linked credit scheme for construction/modernization and expansion of 
cold storages and storages for horticulture produce, expansion of the corpus of 
the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund, launching of a Market Information 
Network and promotion of value addition in agriculture through excise 
exemption and other interventions.

(b) National Agriculture Insurance Scheme (NAIS) or 'Rashtriya Krishi 
BimaYojna' was introduced from 1999-2000 Rabi season by the Government of 
India with a view to enlarging coverage in terms of farmers, crops and risks. 
Under the scheme, funds are released to the Implementing Agency, i.e. General 
Insurance Corporation of India, who settle the indemnity claims based on the 
yield data received from the State/UT Governments. These claims are shared 
between the Central Government and State Government on 50:50 basis. At 
present, the scheme is being implemented by 18 States and 2 Union Territories.

[17 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Statement 
Indian Institute of Astrophysics has established a state-of-the-art and 
world's highest astronomical observatory with a 2-meter class optical/infrared 
telescope at Hanle, South-Eastem Laddakh. The cost of the project for setting 
up the high altitude astronomical observa tory is Rs. 38.49 crores. The setting 
up of the Observatory has been completed. The telescope has already received 
its first astronomical image on the night intervening 26/27 September, 2000. 
The main features of th e Observatory are: (i) the site at Hanle has good 
accessibility round the year; (ii) me telescope, its four focal plane instruments, 
and the dome are remotely controlled from Hosakote, Near Bangalore, through 
a dedicated satellite communication link in the INSAT series of satellites, 
making it the first remotely operated astronomical observatory in the country; 
(iii) the telescope incorporates the latest technological developments in the 
field of telescope fabrication. Most importantly, the instrument is a new 
advanced technology telescope and inco rporates short focal ratio (f/1.75 
primary mirror; f/9 Cassegrain), ultra-low expansion mirror and is able to 
withstand the low temperatures in Hanle (-30 degrees Centigrade), and provide 
high image quality, superb pointing and tracking accuracy.

Saraswati, Hanle, Laddakh has been initiated for inclusion in the Tenth Five

Comprehensive Seed Policy 
*373. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to bring before Parliament a 
comprehensive seed policy or to overhaul the existing Seeds Act, 1966; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) and (b) The 
Government propose to bring forward a comprehensive seed policy and overhaul 
the existing Seeds Act, 1966. This is necessitated by far-reaching changes that 
have taken place in the national economic and agriculture scenario and in the 
international environment since the enactment of the ex isting seeds legislation. 
Moreover special thrust is proposed to be given to production of good quality seed 
in order to meet the food production targets of the future. 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2001] 
The salient features of the proposed seed policy are given below:— 
Varietal Development and Plant Variety Protection 
— An effective sui generis system for intellectual property protection will 
be implemented to stimulate investment in research and development of 
new plant varieties and to facilitate the growth of th> Seed Industry in 
the country. 
Seed production 
—  Steps will be taken to ensure availability of good quality seed in adequate 
quantity. 
—  The 'Seed Village Scheme' will be promoted to facilitate production and 
timely availability of seed of desired crop/ varieties at the local level. Seed 
production will be extended to areas , which are outside the traditional 
seed growing areas.   ' - 
—  Seed Banks will be established for stocking specified quantities of seed of 
required crop/variety for ensuring timely and adequate supply of seeds to 
fanners during adverse conditions. 
Quality Assurance 
—  The Seed Act, 2001 will regulate the sale, import and export of seeds and 
supply of quality seeds to farmers throughout the country. 
—  National Seed Board (NSB) will be established in place of existing Central 
Seed Committee (CSC) and Central Seed Certification Board (CSCB). The 
NSB will have permanent existence with the responsibility of executing 
and implementing the provisions of the Seeds Act and advising the 
Government on all matters relating to seed planning and development etc. The 
Board will function as the apex body in the seed sector. 
Seed distribution and marketing 
—  Private Seed Sector will be encouraged and motivated to restructure and 
reorient their activities for catering to nontraditional areas. 
—  Distribution and marketing of seed of any variety for the purpose of sowing 
and planting will be allowed only if the said variety has been registered by 
the National Seeds Board. National Seed Board may direct a dealer to sell or 
distribute seeds in a specified manner if it is considered necessary to the 
public interest. 
28 

[17 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Infrastructure facilities 
—  Seed processing, storage facilities will be augmented. 
—  Training facilities will be established and a computerized national seed 
grid will be created. 
Transgenic Plant Varieties 
—  All genetically engineered crops/varieties will be tested for 
environmental and bio-safety before their commercial release as per the 
regulations and guidelines of the Environment Protection Act (EPA), 
1986. 
—  The transgenic crops/varieties will be tested to determine their agronomic 
value for at least two seasons under the All India Coordinated Project 
Trials of ICAR. 
Import of seeds and planting material 
— All import of seeds and planting materials, etc. will be allowed freely 
subject to requirements of the Plants , Fruits and Seeds (Regulation of 
import into India) Order, 1989 as amended from time to time. 
Export of Seeds 
— Export of seeds and planting materials will be encouraged through 
promotional programmes and steps will be taken to improve their quality 
and competitiveness to meet the required standards. 
Promotion of domestic seed industry 
— Incentives will be provided to domestic seed industry to encourage and 
promote its growth to enable it to produce seeds of high yielding varieties 
and hybrid seeds at a faster pace to meet the challenges of the domestic 
requirement. 
The salient features of the proposed revised Seeds Act are:— 
—  Establishment of National Seeds Board is proposed in the place of Central 
Seed Committee and Central Seed Certification Board. 
—  Seed of any kind or variety for the purpose of sowing or planting will be 
sold in the country only if the said kind or variety has been registered by 
the National Seeds Board as per the criteria prescribed. 
29 

RAJYA SABHA [ 17 August, 2001 ] 
—  The Government will have the right to exclude certain kind or varieties 
from registration to protect public order or public morality or human, 
animal and plant life and health or to avoid serious prejudice to the 
environment. 
—  National Seeds Board will specify minimum standards on germination, 
genetic and physical purity with respect to any seed of a registered kind 
or variety. 
—  The mark or lable on the seed consignment will indicate that such seed 
conforms to the minimum standards, as specified. 
—  For regulating sale of seeds, no person or dealer will be allowed to carry 
on the business of selling or supplying any seed which is not a registered 
kind/variety. 
—  Farmers will be exempted from the requirement to register their kinds or 
varieties. 
—  National Seeds Board or the State Government may accredit individuals 
or organizations to carry out certification, including self-certification on 
fulfillment of criteria prescribed by the Board. 
—  All seed processing units will require to be registered and to maintain 
minimum specifications. 
—  Import of seed for sale shall be permitted only of registered varieties. 
Registration of such varieties shall be granted on the basis of trial 
conducted from minimum period of 3 seasons in India. 
—  Any person intending to import seed or planting material will declare that 
such materials is, or is not, as the case may be, of transgenic character. 
—  Seed or planting material or transgenic nature will have to carry a 
declaration on their lable to this effect.

*378. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND

MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) A statement is laid on the table of the house. 
Statement 
Details of Major Scientific breakthroughs achieved by India 
A doctor while working at the ma ulana Azad Medical College, New 
Delhi developed a surgical technique for regenerating organs in mammals. It 
has been informed by the inventor that stem cells from body tissues like, 
peritoneum and gut, were selected and colonised with the tissue and organ 
systems in the body using specialised surgical technique. It takes about 2 to 3 
months for the formation of an organ. This is a path breaking achievement as 
this technique has the potential of revolutionalising the medical science as 
one can see the possibility of doing away with organ and tissue transplants. 
No donors are required. As the body forms tissues and organs from its own 
cells, there is no problem of acceptance of foreign body, a problem associated 
with transplants. No post-operative treatment by immundsupressant drugs are 
required as needed in transplant surger y. The application was filed in the US 
Patent and Trademark Office on August 29, 1997 and the patent was granted 
on May 8, 2001. 
The Simputer is a low cost portable alternative device to PC by which 
the benefits of IT can reach the common man. This has been designed and 
developed by the scientists of the Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore. It is 
a hand held computing device. The design goal is to make it usable by people 
who may not be literate. The Simputer o ffers conversion of text to speech. It 
can currently read and speak several Indian languages. Thus, use of simple 
icons to be selected and text to speech output in local language are the primary 
33 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2001] 
means of communication. The user is not  expected to be familiar with the 
currently widespread user interface paradigm like windows, slidebars and pull 
down menus. The projected cost of the Simputer is Rs. 9000/- at large volumes. 
It can take Smart Cards and this enables it to be shared by a community. A 
local community such as the village panchayat, the village school, a kiosk, a 
village postman or even a shopkeeper should be able to loan the device to 
individuals for some length of time and then pass it on to others in the 
community. This would reduce the cost per user. Applications in diverse sectors

Changes in Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 
†*380. SHRI KRTPAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT ANF 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
36 

[ 17 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether it is a fact that developmental activities in Adivasi and tribal 
areas have been adversely affected as a result of implementation of the Forest 
(Conservation) Act, 1980; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) whether Government would consider to make the Act a bit flexible so 
that developmental activities in Adivasi and tribal areas remain unaffected; 
and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (d) Forests provide several usufructs in meeting the sustenance 
and livelihood needs of the tribals including food during lean period. 
Regulation of diversion of forest to non-forestry activity is in the long term 
interest of the tribal and local commun ities. Therefore, Forest (Conservation) 
Act, 1980 helps in safeguarding interests of the Adivasis and tribals rather 
than adversely affecting them. The Act has adequate flexibility to allow the 
activities that are for the welfare of the tribal community without causing 
irreparable damage to the forest eco-system. 
The Act being regulatory and not prohibitory in nature is flexible enough 
to allow important developmental activities on forest lands and as such no 
change or amendment in the Act is contemplated.

2750. SHRIK.M. SAIFULLAH: 
SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether China is seeking Indian expertise on WTO, to enable it to 
join the WTO by November, 2001; 
(b) if so, whether WTO is crippling domestic farmers and experts have 
pointed out a need for revision of agriculture policy; 
(c) whether India and China have seriou s reservations about the impact 
of WTO on agriculture; 
(d) whether India is in touch with the countries, who oppose the WTO; 
and 
(e) what steps India is considering in this regard? 
THEMLNISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OFAGRICULTURE (SHRI 
SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) No, Sir. However, in the various bilateral meetings 
between our delegation and the Chinese delegation held in the context of China's 
accession to WTO, the Chinese side ha ve requested for and have also 
acknowledged receiving our support for the early accession of China to WTO. 
(b) India is a founder member of WTO which came into being on 1.1.1995 
as a successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade 1947 (GATT), of 
which also India was a founder member. The Agreement on Agriculture (AoA) 
is one of the Uruguay Round of Agreements which India had signed at Marrakesh 
in April, 1994. WTO provides predictable rule based multilateral trading system 
which protects the member countries from  pressures of their stronger trading 
partners. By virtue of being a member of WTO, India is automatically entitled to 
get the Most Favoured Nation and National Treatment for its exports. WTO 
also has a strong Dispute Settlement Mechanism to resolve any dispute between 
members. 
(c) Under the Agreement on Agriculture (AoA) India's domestic policy 
options for agricultural and rural development have not by and larg. been 
constrained. However, the countries who were not earlier giving export 
50 

[ 17 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
subsidies during the base period from 1986—1990 are prohibited from giving 
export subsidies. The developing countries, however, have no reduction 
commitments during the implementation period for the subsidies given to 
reduce the cost of marketing, exports including the international and domestic 
freight and handling cargo. The experience of the implementation of the AoA 
has brought out a number of issues, which deserve re-balancing and have 
already been flagged by India in its comprehensive proposals submitted in 
WTO as a part of the continuing mandated negotiations. The Indian proposals 
aim at protecting its food and livelihood security and for creating opportunities 
for the exports of its agricultural surpluses. 
In so far as China is concerned, while media reports have mentioned 
reservations about the adverse impact of WTO agreement on the agriculture 
sector of China, no official statement about this from the Chinese Government 
has come to the notice of Government. 
(d) and (e)As part of the ongoing negotiations under the WTO Agreement 
on Agriculture, India alongwith many other developing countries have 
highlighted the fact that the anticipated benefits of liberalization in agriculture 
have not materialized for them because of the continuation of trade distorting 
subsidies by many of the developed co untries and have, therefore, demanded 
substantial reductions in trade distorting domestic support, substantial 
reductions in tariffs and elimination of export subsidies by the developed 
countries and sufficient flexibility to th e developing countries to take care of 
these food security and livelihood concerns. In this regard, India besides 
submitting detailed proposals in the areas of market access, domestic support, 
export competition and food security, has also co-sponsored two proposals on 
'Market Access' and 'Export Credits' al ongwith other developing countries. 
While the proposal on 'Market Access' was co-sponsored by India alongwith 
Cuba, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Honduras, Kenya, Nigeria, Pakistan, 
Sri Lanka, Uganda, Zimbabwe and Haiti, the proposal on Export Credit was 
co-sponsored alongwith Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, Bolivia, Chile, 
Costa Rica, Guatemala and Malaysia. As  a part of coalition building with 
other developing countries and to garner support for our point of view, the 
Commerce and Industry Minister has written to all the Trade Minister of WTO 
Members of G-77 group of countries with a view to coordinating our positions 
in the context of Doha Ministerial Conference.

2772. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS

THE MINISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS (SHRI SATYA BRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) to (c) Fresh guidelines 
laying down the revised procedure for submission of bills for payment/recoveries 
in respect of sales of de-controlled phosphatic and potassic fertilizers under 
the Concession Scheme have been issued on 17.5.2001 by the Department of 
Fertilizers. To expedite processing of claims as also to reduce the time lag 
between sales and release of concession , the procedure for certification of 
sales has been rationalised. The full text of the revised guidelines is also available 
on Internet (http://fert.nic.in). 
As per the Industrial policy resolution dated 24th July, 1991, no license 
in required for setting up/expansion of fertilizer plants. Entrepreneurs are free to 
set up fertilizer projects anywhere in the country subject to environmental 
acceptance. However, the Government of India has been providing incentives 
for augmenting indigenous fertilizer production which inter-alia include:

of existing units at a concessional rate of custom duty.

fertilizer projects provided such  supplies are made under the 
procedure of international competitive bidding.

rate of custom duty.

Retention Price -cum-Subsidy Scheme (RPS) for urea and 
Concession Scheme for de-controlled fertilizers.

crore are under implementation in the country. When commissioned, these 
projects will create an additional capacity of 3.8 lakh MT per annum of urea and 
6.76 lakh MT per annum of DAP, in the country.

Government announces Maximum Retail Price (MRP) for urea and its production 
is subsidised under the RPS. Consequent to decontrolling and decanalising of 
potassic and phosphatic fertilisers, th e Government introduced Concession 
Scheme from 1992-93, under which concession is being provided on decontrolled 
potassic and phosphatic fertilisers on being sold at MRPs indicated under the 
Scheme. The imports of fertilizers other than urea, whose distribution and 
movement is controlled through ECA allocations, have been put under Open 
General License. The Buffer Scheme for imported MOP is also being implemented.

Statement I  
Gist of major recommendations contained in the Report of the National 
Expert Committee on Women Prisoners headed by Justice Krishna Iyer 
1. Policy Making and Monitoring 
(a) A National Policy on Custodial Justice to women should be formulated 
and adopted. A draft policy was suggested by the Expert Committee. 
(b) National Authority on Custodial Justice to Women (NACJW) should 
be constituted to overview and monitor the implementation of the National 
Policy. 
(c) One Member of NACJW be designated as the Ombudsman for 
Custodial Institution for Women in India. 
2. Judicial 
(a) State level ACJAW and Ombudsman be also set up. 
(b) Depending on the individual preferences of States, either the 
jurisdiction of Family Court constituted under the Family court Act 1984 be 
extended or the Women's Court should be instituted to dispense justice to 
women. But it should be mandatory fo r the States to create a separate and 
specialized justice dispensing modality to women. 
(c) Nari Bandigriha Adalat in the nature of mobile judicial camps for 
rendering speedy redress to women in custody. 
 
89 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2001] 
3. Legislative 
(a) Article 252 of the Constitution of India should be invoked to get the 
concurrence of two or more States to bring uniform Comprehensive Prison and 
Prisoner Act throughout the country. 
(b) A comprehensive code to cover the administration of all custodial 
institutions should also be formulated. 
 
(c) Critical assessment of the effi cacy and relevance of various 
legislations bearing on women's status in custody and their criminality should 
be undertaken by the Law Commission. 
(d) Appropriate amendment should be made in the IPC, Cr. PC, Prison 
Act, 1894 and Police Act 1861 to reflect the special needs of women in custody. 
(e) The new Mental Health Bill should reflect the specific 
recommendations of the Committee in respect of the custody and treatment of 
non-criminal and criminal lunatic women. 
4. Administrative 
A, Prisons 
(a) A cadre of prison service should be set up. 
(b) There should be enhanced and protected representation of women in 
the prison cadre. 
(c) There should be women DIG at the State HQ preferably from prison 
service to look after the work relating to women prisons. 
 
(d) Women Superintendents of Women prisons should be made fully 
autonomous. 
(e) There should be permanent wardens and matrons. 
(f) Prisoner's Council should be set up in every prison. 
(g) Socio-legal counseling cells should be set up in every prison 
(h) Released Prisoner's Aid Societies should operate in every district. 
(i) Prison amenities for women and their children should be clearly 
identified preferably in a separate volume of the Prison Manual.

JOSHI): (a) and (b) National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT), Chennai

Committee; 
143 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2001] 
(b) the reasons necessitating the appointment of such a Committee, the 
procedure presently being followed in electrification projects; and 
(c) by when the report of this Committee is expected to be received? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) Yes, Sir. The Committee will evolve an appropriate 
criteria including norms for sensitivity analysis for taking up electrification 
projects over the next three Plan periods, i.e. upto the year 2016-17. In evolving 
these criteria, the Committee shall take into account the following:— 
(i) The total availability of energy (both electrical and petroleum) in the 
country and its optimum utilization between different sectors, based 
on energy efficiency; 
(ii) The priority that needs to be given for use of electric energy for 
traction purposes by the Indian Ra ilways, taking into account the 
total capital requirement involved; 
(iii) The capabilities of the two trac tion systems to handle longer/heavier 
passenger/freight trains at higher average/ maximum speeds, but 
operating within the operational a nd infrastructural constraints of 
Indian Railways. 
(iv) Cost to the Organisation caused by a redudancy of existing assets/ 
manpower; coupled with associated benefits derived as a result of 
electrification like reliable power s upply over the electrified route, 
impact on environments, etc; and 
(v) The present methodology of worki ng out of the line haul costs, 
suggest improvements and propose the most viable norms including 
fixing a break even point. The Committee shall evaluate the actual 
rate of return achieved on 3 re presentative electrification projects 
(high density, moderate density and low density) completed more 
than 5 years ago and compare this w ith the projected rate of return 
when the project was proposed. 
(b) Considerable progress has been  made in the field of Railway 
Electrification, in the recent past. Time has now come for a comprehensive 
review of the process and also for evolving a clear plan for the future, keeping 
in view all aspects of Railway working as well as environmental factors affecting 
the choice of traction. It has, therefore, been decided to constitute a Committee 
for determining the norms for further electrification over the next three Plan 
periods.

at Unmanned level crossings are listed below:—

level crossing so that road vehicle drivers reduce their speed.

drivers to whistle from the whistle board till such time as the train 
passes the level crossing gate.

publicity campaings through media like quickies on TV, cinema slides, 
posters, talks on radio, newspaper advertisements and street plays.

Act, 1988 and the Railways Act, 1989.

programmes.

and at retail petrol pumps.

Controversial clinical trial conducted in Regional Cancer Centre, 
Thiruvananthapuram 
SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN (Kerala): Sir, I would like to draw 
the attention of this House to a controversial clinical trial conducted by the 
Regional Cancer Centre in collaboratio n with the Johns Hopkins University, 
Baltimore, U.S. It has become a serious controversy receiving international 
media attention that banned drugs are applied on patients in connection with a 
clinical study on oral cancer in  the Regional Cancer Centre, 
Thiruvananthapuram, in collaboration with the Johns Hopkins University of 
the United States. Poor patients in the RCC are alleged to have .been 
subjected to the trial which exposes them to toxicity from drugs which stand 
banned by the Federal Drugs Administration (FDA) in the United States. The 
substance used on the patients was the tetra methyl form of Nor Dihydro 
Gauceretic Acid (NGDA). The M4N developed by the Johns Hopkins 
University  is in the unsafe category of the FDA. 
This act is in total violation of the ethical and moral conventions of 
administering experimental medicines. Even a sanction from the Drugs 
Controller General of India is not obtained. 
The entire episode had a new turn yesterday when the Johns Hopkins 
University, in its press release through website, stated that they have not 
entrusted to any agency the conduct of the study on this medicine and hence 
they have ordered an inquiry. 
Since the matter is getting new dimensions of such a grave nature, 
the intervention of the Government of India becomes inevitable and hence an 
immediate inquiry is to be conducted into this matter. I would just add this, 
Sir.   I understand that an inquiry has already been conducted by the 
174

Heroes of Goa Liberation Struggle 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA (West Bengal): Sir. thank you 
very much for giving me this opportunity. Sir, my Special Mention is with 
regard to the history of Goa Liberation Struggle. Sir, I regret drawing the 
attention of this august House and the concerned Ministry of the Government 
of India regarding the utter neglect of important sites of the history of our 
anti-imperialist struggle. The Goa liberation struggle of the fifties has been an 
epoch-making episode in the annals of history of our anti-colonial struggle. 
The renowned leaders, namely, Tridib Kumar Chawdhury, Madhu Limaye, 
Ananta Joshi, Nana Saheb Goray etc. were put behind the Portugese prison, 
Aguada Fort, Goa. Most of them were detained in cell No. 13 of the said jail 
from July 1955 to February 1957. Th e bravery, sacrifice and commitment of 
the leaders were acclaimed by the nation,  and they were accorded a hero's 
reception. At last, Goa was liberated fro m the Portugese colonial rule. In the 
independent Goa, the Aguada Fort jail was converted into a central jail. It is a 
pity on our part that not even a plaque, depicting the history of the struggle, 
could be seen near or inside cell No. 13 or inside the jail. The same cell, 
where the noble freedom fighters we re detained, now accommodates the 
hardcore criminals and drug peddlars. On inquiry, I found that some old 
patriots still assemble once a year to offer homage to the freedom fighters, 
who had sacrificed their lives. 
I demand of the concerned Ministry to appropriately correct the 
situation and raise a monument to commemorate the anti-imperialist struggle 
by inscribing the names of those valiant fighters so that the values of selfless 
sacrifices could be imbibed by the people of this country. Thank you.

SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE (Assam): Sir, I would

nexus between the Railway authorities and the powerful road transport lobby, 
which is affecting the progress in completing the work of gauge conversion in

the operating staff so that the public becomes disgusted while travelling by 
train and give up the mode of travelling by train. I, therefore, plead with the 
Railway Minister to kindly institute a high-level inquiry into the matter so that 
this unholy nexus is put to an end to in the public interest. Thank you.

Magasasay Award recognition to Indian National Wisdom 
PROF. (SHRIMATI) BHARATI RAY (West Bengal): Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, I would like to draw the attention of the House to an event of 
unusual national importance. Usually, we discuss the problems of our 
country. We also need to highlight the positive aspects of our country as well, 
like the silent work done by brilliant but relatively unknown people. Rajendra 
Singh has won the Magasasay Award this year. It is a recognition of Indian 
traditional wisdom and needs to be celebrated. Water is going to be the rarest 
commodity in the world including India. Unless we discover a cheap way to 
desalinise seawater, we shall have to  say like Coleridge, "Water, Water 
everywhere, not a drop to drink". The only way of survival is rainwater 
harvesting. This is what Rajendra Singh has reportedly done by adopting two 
strategies. First, he constructed at Alwar in Rajasthan small dams, not in the 
style of big dams constructed with we stern technology, but in the traditional 
indigenous manner. Secondly, he accomplished it neither with money power 
nor with the Government's assistance. He involved the commu iity and built 
awareness among them about the value of  water and about the value of joint 
community work. Consequently, Alwar suffered no drought ; with crops 
growing, forest becoming greener and four dead rivers brought back to life. 
I urge upon the Minister of Water Resources to take note of it and 
extend support to indigenous experiments in other parts of India as well. 
Water needs maximum attention not only of the States but also of the Centre. 
Indigenous methods of rainwater harvesting and community involvement and 
community participation need national support. 
Thank you.

of postal stamp in memory of Shri Pingali Venkaiah, the creator of our 
Tricolour

Chairman, 
180 

[17 Augufct, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Sir, I am requesting the Government to  erect a statue in the premises of 
Parliament and release a postal stamp in memory of Shri Pingali Venkaiah, 
the creator of our Tricolour. 
Pingali Venkaiah, a Gandhian, the creator of our nation's Tricolour 
that gave enthusiasm, exuberance and patriotism to our countrymen in 
achieving our independence, died in poverty in a small hut in Vijayawada, 
Andhra Pradesh. His only and ultimate dream was to look at the National 
Flag, designed by him, fluttering at the ramparts of the Red Fort. But the most 
pitiable thing is, neither he nor his family members could afford to take him 
to Delhi to see his National Flag flying' from the Red Fort. He died in such a 
pitiable condition. Is this the recognition that we are giving to a great freedom 
fighter? He met Mahatma Gandhi in South Africa and since then had a very 
close association with him. Our beloved leader, Dr. N.T, Rama Rao, had put 
up a statue of this patriot at the Tank Bund, Hyderabad, Andhra Pradesh. 
The most astonishing thing is that the Central Government has 
neither sanctioned any freedom fighter pension nor any other benefit to his 
family members. The result is : The whole family of our great patriot 
disintegrated and little is known about his two sons and a daughter. The only 
known survivor of this family is his daughter. I think she is earning her 
livelihood by selling papads and pickle. I request the Government to 
immediately sanction pension to the fam ily members of the architect of the 
Tricolour and a lesson depicting his history should be introduced in the 
curriculum of the textbooks. I also request the Government to erect a statue in 
the premises of Parliament and release a postal stamp which will be a 
befitting tribute to the great leader. Thank you.

REVIEW OF NATIONAL EDUCATION POLICY, 1966 
PROF. (SHRIMATI) BHARATI RAY (West Bengal): Sir, I move 
the following Resolution:- 
“That this House recommends that the National Education Policy, 
1986 be reviewed." 
Sir, we are facing a crisis in the field of education. It is time, 
therefore, to concentrate on the Education Policy, and more specifically, on 
the implementation of the policy that we have. We had a National Education 
Policy passed by Parliament in 1986. It was modified by Parliament in 1992, 
and we also had an Approved Plan of Action, 1992. The NEP provided for 
"monitoring and review" every five years. A Central Advisory Board of 
Education was envisaged in the NEP "as a body to play a pivotal role in 
reviewing the educational developments, determining the changes required to 
improve the system and monitoring implementation." But today, we have 
come to a point when crucial decisions are being taken without consulting 
Parliament. If reviews have to be made, they have to be transparent. Well-
known scholars and intellectuals from different branches of knowledge have to 
be consulted. Professionals have to be involved to identify the lacunae and 
find out ways and means to rectify them. 
Sir, education is a vast subject. In this short time at my disposal, I 
will mention only a few points. The NEP emphasises on the universal access, 
universal enrolment and universal retention of all children up to 14 years. 
"Education is for all."  But, see, not even illiteracy has been removed, 
241 

RAJYA SABHA [17 August, 2001] 
23 million boys and 36 millions girls are out of school. Crores of rupees are 
spent on various schemes, but there is no monitoring, no evaluation. In fact, 
the bulk of our children enrolled in schools are first generation learners. What 
steps have the Government taken to enable them to develop an understanding 
of their physical and social environm ent? A majority of students live in 
villages. What is the percentage of the total education budget for education in 
rural areas? Most schools do not have drinking water facility. Some do not 
have even a lavatory. Schools are an assemblage for parrots. The curriculum 
needs to be modernised. But how? Not by introducing Jyotir Vigyan or Vedic 
Mathematics? The curriculum should be addressed to the requirements of the 
life-situations of our students. 
Coming to vocational education, in the NPE 1986, it was stated 4hat 
'Voctional education will be a distinct stream, intended to prepare students for 
identified occupations spanning several areas of activity'. Concern was shown 
for women and the disadvantaged sections in the society. What was not 
detailed out in the NPE was how the vocational education was to be imparted; 
which course, at what level, in what form, was to be imparted at which places, 
and for what sections of people? You must see what kind of skills are needed 
in specific areas, what kind of technici ans are needed where,  what the market 
potentials are. Otherwise, how would you ensure that the students who get 
vocational education are employed or become self-employed? Unless jobs are 
assured, or alternatively, there is scope, and demand for products that a self-
employed person can offer, who will go in for vocational education? 
Vocational training should be imparted on practical lines. The education 
policy must spell out the detailed methodology. 
Coming to higher education, the UGC has not done its job at all. 
Now it is reconstituted with members and people, I am sorry to say, who are 
relatively unknown. That is the mildest term I can use, "relatively unknown". 
The NPE says, "Efforts will be made to delve into India's ancient fund of 
knowledge and to relate it to contemporary reality." But see, we are busy 
trying to introduce Vedic Mathematics, it had its place in history, but it has no 
relationship to modern development process. There is a Report given by the 
CAG that the number of international standards of research is decreasing, the 
number of patenting by Indian scholars is going down. Shall we introduce 
astrology and Vedic Mathematics, and impose a burden
