OFFICE MEMORANDUM 
Subject: Guidelines for qualification of Bidders seeking to acquire stakes in 
Public Sector Enerprises through the process of disinvestment 
Government has examined the issue of framing comprehensive and 
transparent quidelines defining the criteria for bidders interested in PSE-
disinvestment so that the parties selected through competitive bidding could 
inspire public confidence. Earlier, criteria like net worth, experience etc. used 
to be prescribed. Based on experience and in consultation with concerned 
departments, Government has decided to prescribe the following additional 
criteria for the qualification/disqualification of the parties seeking to acquire 
stakes in public sector enterprises through disinvestment:—  
(a) In regard to matters other than the security and integrity of the country, 
any conviction by a Court of Law or indicitment/adverse order by a 
regulatory authority that casts a doubt on the ability of the bidder to 
manage the public sector unit when it is disinvested, or which relates 
to a grave offence would constitute disqualification. Grave offence is 
defined to be of such a nature that it outrages the moral sense of the 
community. The decision in regard to the nature of the offence would 
be taken on case to case basis afte r considering the facts of the case 
and relevant legal principles, by the Government. 
(b) In regard to matters relating to the security and integrity of the country, 
any charge-sheet by an agency of the Government/ conviction by a 
Court of Law for an offence committed by the bidding party or by any 
sister concern of the bidding party would result in disqualification. 
The decision in regard to the relationship between the sister concerns 
13 

RAJYA SABHA [20 August, 2001] 
would be taken, based on the relevant facts and after examining whether the 
two concerns are substantially controlled by the same person/ persons. 
(c) In both (a) and (b), disqualification shall continue for a period that 
Government deems appopriate. 
(d) Any entity, which is disqualified from participating in the 
disinvestment process, would not be allowed to remain associated with 
it or get associated merely because it has preferred an appeal against the 
order based on which it has been disqualified. The mere pendency of 
appeal will have no effect on the disqualification. 
(e) The disqualification criteria would come into effect immediately and 
would apply to all bidders for various disinvestment transactions, which 
have not been completed as yet. 
(0 Before disqualifying a concern, a Show Cause Notice why it should not 
be disqualified would be issued to it and it would be given an 
opportunity to explain its position. 
(g) Henceforth, these criteria will be prescribed in the advertisements seeking 
Expression of Interest (EOI) from the interested parties. The interested 
parties would be required to provide the information on the above 
criteria, along with their Expressions of Interest (EOI). The bidders shall 
be required to provide with their EOI an undertaking to the effect that no 
investigation by a regulatory authority is pending against them. In case any 
investigation in pending against the concern or its sister concern or 
against its CEO or any of its Directors/ Managers/employees, full 
details of such investigation including the name of the investigating 
agency, the charge/offence for which the investigation has been 
launched, name and designation of persons against whom the 
investigation has been launched and other relevant information should be 
disclosed, to the satisfaction of the Government. For other criteria also, a 
similar undertaking shall be obtained along with EOI.

[20 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (c) As per the information given by the State Drug Control 
Authorities, 17 cases related to spurious drugs have been reported from Delhi, 
Rajasthan, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and U.R 
in last one year (Statement-I) (See below) 68 persons have been arrested in 
this regard since 1.4.2000 (Statement-U), (See below). 
Under the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules 
thereunder. State Governments have been empowered to enforce quality of 
drugs including check on manufacture or sale of spurious drugs. The said Act 
was amended in 1982 to provide for specific definition of spurious drugs and 
severe penalties extending to life imprisonment have been prescribed. 
State Governments have been advised from time to time to provide 
adequate enforcement machinery and drug te sting facilities and to keep strict 
surveillance over the inter-state moveme nt of spurious drugs. Facilities of 
Central Government testing labs have also been made available to the States 
for testing of drugs besides financial assistance provided to them to augment 
and strengthen their testing capabilities. 
The State Drugs Controllers have been advised to take the following 
measures for curbing the incidence of spurious drugs:—  
(i) Constitution/reactivation of St ate Drug Advisory Committees in 
which various trade and industry association as well as consumer 
association should find representation. 
(ii) Establishment of separate in telligence-cum-legal machinery with 
police assistance. 
(iii) Training to be provided to selected Officials of Drug Control 
Administration in the modalities of intelligence work, prosecution 
etc. in respect of Spurious/Counterfeit drugs. 
(iv) To ensure speedy analysis of drugs samples by establishing own 
state level drug testing facilities. 
(v) State Drugs Control Authorities to be cautious while approving 
licences for drug products to ensure that "look-alike" products axe 
not encouraged. 
(vi)   To develop efficient communication facilities and recall procedures. 
(vii)   To undertake surveillance of suspected dealers.

In addition, the following steps have been taken:—  
(i) Association of Pharmaceutical In dustry and All India Organisation 
of Chemists and Druggists have been asked to take necessary 
initiative to collectively combat the menace of spurious drugs. 
(ii) The problem of manufacture and sale of spurious drugs and the need

menace of Spurious drugs and suggest remedial measures.

Procedure adopted for permission of new drugs 
*389. SHRI MUNAVVAR HASAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the procedure being adopted for the permission of new drugs; 
(b) the normal time taken for the grant of permission for the new drugs; 
(c) the names of the new drugs for which permission has been granted 
during this year; and 
(d) the time taken in each case? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (d) The requirement for evaluation of a new drug application 
for market authorisation are prescribed under rules 122A to E and Schedule 
'Y' of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945. The modalities inter-alia include 
initial evaluation of chemical and physical characterstics, animal toxicity, 
pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the drug. This evaluation is done 
by the office of the DCG(I) with the help of experts. It also involves approval 
of protocols for clinical trials as well as scrutiny of data generated by various 
clinical trials and result of the testing of the new drug by the Central Government 
Laboratories. 
This evaluation of a new drug application is a complex process. The 
time taken varies according to the natu re of the molecule/drug and depending 
upon the nature of the application. It may normally take more than five years 
for approval of Investigational New Drug (a drug molecule not tested on 
human beings anywhere in the world), about 1-3 years for the first time 
approval in India of a drug already approved elsewhere and about 2-3 months 
for subsequent applications by other manufacturers for drugs already approved 
for market authorisation in India. This is, however, subject to timely 
submission of all required data as per provision of Schedule 'Y' of the Drugs 
and Cosmetics Rules by the applicant.  Certain categories of the drugs, viz. 
anti-cancer, anti-AIDS, etc. are examined on a fast track mode. 
A list of New Drugs approved this year (1st Jan. 2001 to 30th June 
2001) is annexed as statement.

Problem of spurious drugs 
*393. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned "Even the Chemist does not know which one is fake" which appeared 
in me Times of India, dated me 7th July, 2001; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) the s'teps proposed to be taken to control the problem of spurious 
drugs flooding the market? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. Govern ment are aware mat the manufacture, 
sale and distribution of spurious drugs, a clandestine illegal activity, is indulged 
in by some unscrupulous and anti-social persons. 
Under the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules 
mereunder, State Governments have been empowered to enforce quality of 
drugs including check on manufacture or sale of spurious drugs. The said Act 
was amended in 1982 to provide for specific definition of spurious drugs and 
severe penalties extending to life imprisonment have been prescribed. 
State Governments have been advised from time to time to provide 
adequate enforcement machinery and drug testing facilities and to keep strict 
surveillance over the inter-state moveme nt of spurious drugs. Facilities of 
Central Government testing labs have also been made available to the States 
for testing of drugs besides financial assistance provided to them to augment 
and strengthen their testing capabilities. 
The Drugs Controller General (India) has advised the State Drugs Controller 
to take the following measures for curbing the incidence of spurious drugs: 
(i) Constitution/reactivation of St ate Drug Advisory Committees in 
which various trade and industry association as well as consumer 
association should find representation. 
(ii) Establishment of separate in telligence-cum-legal machinery with 
police assistance. 
(iii) Training to be provided to selected Officials of Drug Control 
Administration in the modalities of intelligence work, prosecution 
etc. in respect of Spurious/Counterfeit drugs. 
50 

[20 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(iv) To ensure speedy analysis of drugs samples by establishing own 
state level drug testing facilities. 
(v) State Drugs Control Authorities to be cautious while approving 
licences for drug products to ensure  that "look-alike" products are 
not encouraged. 
(vi)    To develop efficient communication facilities and recall procedures. 
(vii)    To undertake surveillance of suspected dealers. 
(viii)    To engage experienced counsel for fighting spurious drug cases. 
(ix) To obtain Cooperation of Ph armaceutical Industry by regular 
interaction with them. 
(x) To collect survey samples under Naitonal Survey Quality Evaluation 
of Drug (NSQED) programme. 
In addition, the following steps have been taken:—  
(1) The All India Organisation of Chemist and Druggist Association 
(AIOCD) holds National Pharmacy Weeks from time to time to create 
awareness among the public. Do's and Donot's for consumers are also 
published. 
(2) The Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has constituted a 
Committee under the Chairmanship of DGHS on July 18,2001 to go 
into all aspects of the menace of Spurious drugs and suggest remedial 
measures. 
(3) The problem of manufacture and sale of spurious drugs and the need 
to ensure its checking has been specifically explained to State Health 
Ministers during the meeting of Central Council of Health & Family 
Welfare.

tuberculosis infections.

Effective implementation of Population Control Programmes 
† 2917. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the economic development of the country is 
not in proportion to the growth of population in the country; and 
(b) if so, the steps Government propose to take to effectively implement 
the population control programmes and to make them more effective? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) The objective of the National Family 
Welfare Programme is to reduce the birth rate to the extent necessary to stabilise 
the population at a level consistent with the requirement of the national 
economy. The achievements made under the programme since its inception in 
1952 is quite substantial, but not sufficient. 
Actual success in containing the growth of population is dependent on: 
• Publicly stated support by the community leaders 
• Resources available for the family welfare programme  
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
78 

[20 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
• Efficiency and accountability in th e state health system for ensuring 
effective delivery of services to citizens. 
• Women education and women's status in the family.  
All these inputs have been only partially available and this is the reason 
why the results so far have been only partial. 
(b) Government has adopted National Population Policy, 2000 and in 
February, 2000 which states three objectives. 
The immediate objective of the National Population Policy is to address 
the unmet needs of contrace ption, health infrastructure, health personnel and 
to provide integrated service delivery for basic reproductive and child health 
care. The medium term objective is to bring the total fertility rates to 
replacement level by 2010, through vigorous implementation of inter sectoral 
operational strategies. The long term objective is to achieve a stable population 
by 2045, at a level consistent with the requirements of sustainable economic 
growth, social development and environmental protection. 
It lists National Socio-demographic goals to be achieved by 2010. It 
also enumerates 12 strategies w ith action plan. The Policy is being 
implemented.

the public and service providers aware of the provisions of the Act. The States/ 
UTs have also been advised to provide protection to social activists and Non 
Governmental Organisations giving information or filing complaints of

all the States/UTs have also been addressed recently for following up on 
implementation of various provisions of the PNDT Act.

being involved to carry out projects regarding creating awareness about the 
provisions of the Act. Grant-in-aid has also been released to NGOs to conduct 
seminars and workshops and other Information, Education and Communication 
(TEC) activities in certain States. 
National Level Non-Governmental Organisations have been requested 
to take up projects for generating awareness about the provisions of the Act, 
among doctors/clinics/law enforcing authorities and public at large. The co-
operation of the NGOs has also been requested in listing and enumerating 
within their jurisdiction, the name and address of premises where the Medical 
Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) is being performed, with a view to detect 
registered/unregistered clinics. 
Recently, Supreme Court has issued certain directions to both the Central 
and State Governments for effective implementation of the provisions of the 
PNDT Act. The directions include among other things wide publicity both at 
national and state levels for generating awareness about the Act.

2926. SHRI A. VUAYA RAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware about the increasing level of 
malnutrition problem and related diseases in the country; 
(b) if so, die details uiereof; and 
(c) the steps taken by Government to eradicate such problems? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) The malnutrition levels in 
87 

RAJYA SABHA [20 August, 2001] 
the country are not increasing. Levels have been gradually reducing as per the 
facts given below:- 
 Protein energy malnutrition in children has been reduced from 68.6% 
in 1988-90 to 47.0% in 1998-99. 
 Vitamin A deficiency as indicated by Bitot spot has reduced from 1.8% 
in children during the year 1975-79 to 1.1% in the year 1994-95 
 Prevalence of goitre has reduced from 21.0% in 1989 to 10% in 
1994 
 Iron deficiency anaemia in pregnant women has reduced from 87.5% 
in 1989 to 84.9% in 1999. 
 Chronic energy deficiency in adults has reduced from 51.8% in 
females and 55.6% in males in 1975-79 to 36.3% in females and 
28.6% in males in the year 1995-96. 
(c) The Government of India adopted the National Nutrition Policy in 
1993 which advocated a multisectoral approach for contro lling the problem 
of malnutrition and improving nutritional status of the people. The National 
Nutrition Policy contains both short term/direct interventions and long-
term/indirect interventions. A National Plan of Action on Nutrition was 
developed to serve as a frame-work for translating the instruments of National 
Nutrition Policy which identified the role of 14 Departments/Ministries of the 
Govt, towards nutrition promotion. 
 Various measures adopted by the Government to improve the 
nutritional status of the population are:—  
 Increased agricultural production 
 Improving the purchasing power of the people through income 
generating schemes; 
 Availability of essential food items at subsidised cost through public 
distribution system. 
 Nutrition education to increase the awareness and bringing about the 
desired changes in the feeding practices including promotion of 
breast feeding; 
 Supplementary feeding programmes viz. (i) Integrated Child 
Development Services (ICDS) scheme; (ii) Special Nutrition 
Programme (SNP); (iii) Balwadi Nu trition Programme (BNP); (iv) 
Wheat Based Supplementary Nutrition Programme; (v) Mid-Day 
Meal Programme. 

[20 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
 
 Pradhan Mantri Gramoday a Yojana (PMGY). 
 
 Programmes for prevention of specific nutrient deficiency disorders 
such as National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme; 
Prophylaxis Programme to prevent blindness due to Vitamin A 
deficiency and Nutritional Anaemia due to Iron Deficiency as a part of 
Reproductive and Child Health Programme. 
 
 Pilot Project for control of micronutrient malnutrition is also under 
implementation.

Seizure of spurious drugs 
†2932. SHRI JHUMUK LAL BHENDIA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the steps Government have taken to curb the trade of spurious and 
sub-standard medicines in various parts of the country; 
(b) the States including Delhi where action has been taken against die 
manufacturers of spurious medicines; 
(c) the worth of the spurious medicines seized during die last two years, 
State-wise; and 
(d) the details of die action taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. 
THAKUR): (a) Under die provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and 
Rules mere under, State Governments have been empowered to enforce quality 
of drugs including check on manufacture or sale of spurious drugs. The said 
Act was amended in 1982 to provide for specific definition of spurious drugs 
and severe penalties extending to life imprisonment have been prescribed. 
State Governments have been advised from time to time to provide 
adequate enforcement machinery and drug testing facilities and to keep strict 
surveillance over die inter-state moveme nt of spurious drugs. Facilities of 
Central Government testing labs have also been made available to the States 
for testing of drugs besides financial assistance provided to diem to augment 
and strengthen their testing capabilities. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
99 

RAJYA SABHA [20 August, 2001] 
The State Drugs Controllers have been advised to take the following 
measures for curbing the incidence of spurious drugs:—  
(i) Constitution/reactivation of Stat e Drug Advisory Committees in 
which various trade and industry association as well as consumer 
association should find representation. 
(ii) Establishment of separate in telligence-cum-legal machinery with 
police assistance. 
(iii) Training to be provided to selected Officials of Drug Control 
Administration in the modalities of intelligence work, prosecution 
etc. in respect of Spurious/Counterfeit drugs. 
(iv) To ensure speedy analysis of drugs samples by establishing own 
state level drug testing facilities. 
(v) State Drugs Control Authorities to be cautious while approving 
licenses for drug products to ensure that "look-alike" products are 
not encouraged. 
(vi) To develop efficient communication facilities and recall procedures. 
(vii) To undertake surveillance of suspected dealers. 
(viii) To engage experienced counsel for fighting spurious drug cases. 
(ix) To obtain Cooperation of Ph armaceutical Industry by regular 
interaction with them. 
(x) To collect survey samples under National Survey Quality Evaluation 
of Drug (NSQED) programme. 
In addition, the following steps have been taken: 
(i) Association of Pharmaceutical I ndustry and All India Organisation 
of Chemists and Druggists have been asked to take necessary initiative 
to collectively combat the menace of spurious drugs. 
(ii) The problem of manufacture and sale of spurious drugs and the need 
to ensure its checking has been specifically explained to State Health 
Ministers during the meeting of Central Council of Health and Family 
Welfare. 
100 

[20 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(iii) The Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has constituted a 
Committee under the Chairmanship of DGHS on July 18, 2001 
associating members from Indu stry, Trade, Drugs Regulatory 
Officials and Public representatives to go into all aspects of the 
menace of Spurious drugs and suggest remedial measures. 
(b) As per the information given by the State Drug Control Authorities, 
17 cases related to spurious drugs have been reported from Delhi, Rajasthan, 
Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh in 
last one year. 68 persons have been arrested in this regard during the period 
2000-2001. 
(c) and (d) As per the information given by the State Drug Control 
Authorities of Delhi, 76 allopathic medicines worth Rs. 1 Crore (approx) and 
two Ayurvedic medicines worth Rs. 1.5 crore (Approx) of various manufacturers 
were seized during a raid conducted in July 2001 in and around Bhagirath 
Place in Delhi and At Murtha l, District Sonepat, Haryana. So far Police have 
arrested six persons in this connection and investigations are in progress.

Policy on film finance 
2958. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of 
INFORMATIONAND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that banks have  now authorized to finance film 
makers to the tune of 50 per cent subject to certain terms and conditions 
stipulated in a policy laid down by Government; and 
(b) if so, the details of the policy and will it be subject to approval of the 
Censor Board? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. RBI & IDBI have 
formulated guidelines for banks and financial institutions to finance the film 
128 

[20 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
industry respectively. According to the scheme evolved by IDBI the financial 
institutions will initially focus on financing film production activity of 
corporate entities. While there is no upper limit for sanction, the minimum 
quantum of assistance would normally be not less than Rs. 20 million. The 
quantum of assistance would not exceed 50% of the budget, the debt-equity 
ratio would not exceed 1:1 and the promot er's contribution has to be at.least 
30 per cent of the estimated budget. Part of the equity contribution, not 
exceeding 20 per cent of the estimated budget can be raised in the form of 
advances from distributors against sale of territories music/video rights etc. 
The period of repayment of loan would not exceed two years and loans would 
be sanctioned against various forms of securities specified in the scheme. 
Under the RBI scheme, Banks may provide finance to film producers 
(corporate as well as non-corporate en tities) with good track record in the 
relevant field. Banks may also provide finance to these entities for production 
of films in participation with National Film Development Corporation Limited. 
Banks can finance up to 50 per cent of the project cost on merits. Producers 
are required to bring in at least 35 to  40 per cent of the budget of the film. 
Banks may provide finance to such projects where the total cost of production 
of a film does not exceed Rs. 10 crores. 
The period of loan under this scheme may be fixed based on the financing 
bank's assessment of cash generation of the project. While these are the broad 
guidelines, the banks are free to advance loans based on their own experience 
and other relevant information keeping in view the spirit of the guidelines. 
Approval of the Central Board of Film Certification has to be obtained 
before public exhibition of a film.

Collapse of civil and criminal Justice System 
2960. SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: Will the Minister of LAW, JUSTICE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is a total collapse in civil and criminal 
justice system and the conviction rate is hardly 7 per cent whereas 93 per cent 
of those charged with various crimes go scot-free; 
(b) whether Government have studied and analysed the reasons for 
collapse in justice which encouraged crime becoming a low risk job; 
(c) the steps Government propose to take to ensure speedy conviction of 
criminals and justice to aggrieved parties; 
(d) whether any comprehensive judicial reforms are under consideration; 
and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
ARUN JAJTLEY): (a) No, Sir. 
As per information made available by the National Crime Records Bureau, 
Ministry of Home Affairs, the average conviction rate of crimes under the Indian 
Penal Code from the year 1995 to 1999 has been 39.02%. 
(b) The reasons for poor conviction rate, inter alia, can be attributed to 
the nature of the procedural laws, practices and procedures followed by criminal 
courts and the inadequacies of the investigating and prosecuting agencies. 
(c) to (e) Various steps have been taken by the Government for the speedy 
disposal of both civil and criminal cases. These include amendment of the 
Civil Procedure Code and the Code of Criminal Procedure, increase in the 
number of posts of Judges/Judicial Officers, establishment of Special Courts/ 
tribunals, computerisation of courts and adoption of alternative modes of dispute 
130 

[20 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
resolution, such as, arbitration and conciliation. Lok Adalats have been given 
a statutory base as supplementary forum for resolution of disputes. 
As regards Criminal Procedure Code, the Law Commission of India has 
comprehensively reviewed the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The 
Government has recently appointed a Committee under the chairmanship of 
Shri Justice V.S. Malimath, to suggest measures for revamping the Criminal 
Justice System. 
Government has sanctioned a scheme involving an amount of Rs. 502.90 
crore for creation of 1734 Fast Track C ourts for expeditious disposal of long 
pending sessions cases and cases involving undertrials in jails, on priority. 
The scheme is in operation with effect from April, 2001.

(b) to (d) As regards amendment of Criminal Procedure Code, the Code 
of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 1994 introduced in the Rajya Sabha 
on 9th August, 1994 has, inter alia, the following proposals to provide for 
speedy disposal of cases:—  
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
131 
 

RAJYA SABHA [20 August, 2001 ] 
(i) Clause 26. The proviso to section 223 of the Code of Criminal 
Procedure, 1973 provides that the Magistrate on an application of the accused 
persons may direct their joint trial even if they do not fall in the categories 
specified, if he is satisfied that such persons would not be prejudicially affected 
thereby. In the interest of prompt disposal of cases, scope of this proviso is 
being widen to enable to the Court of Sessions also to hold such trials. 
(ii) Clause 27. Under section 228 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 
1973, a Sessions Judge can transfer a case only to the Chief Judicial Magistrate. 
The proposed amendment seeks to give discretion to the Sessions Judge to 
transfer the case to the Chief Judicial Magistrate or to any other Judicial 
Magistrate of the First Class and to fix a date for the appearance of the accused 
before the Chief Judicial Magistrate or  the Judicial Magistrate, as the case 
may be, so that a lot of time, which is wasted in summoning the accused by 
the Magistrate, may be saved. 
(iii) Clause 28. Under sub-section (1 ) of section 260 of the Code of 
Criminal Procedure, 1973 a Magistrate has a discretion to try offences specified 
therein either summarily or in a regular way. It is proposed to amend this sub-
section to make summary trial of offences specified therein mandatory. It is 
also proposed to provide that the offence of theft and other cognizable offences, 
namely, offences under sections 379,. 380, 381, 411 and 414 of the Indian 
Penal Code, 1860 may be tried summarily where the value of the property 
involved does not exceed two thousand rupees instead of two hundred rupees 
at present. 
The Government of India has also set up a Committee under the 
chairmanship of Justice V.S. Malimath to suggest measures to revamp Criminal 
Justice System in the country. The Report of the Committee is awaited. 
At present, there is no proposal to amend the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. 
In addition to above, various steps have been taken by the Government* 
for the speedy disposal of both civil and criminal cases. These include 
amendment of the Civil Procedure Code and the Code of Criminal Procedure, 
increase in the number of posts of Judges/Judicial Officers, establishment of 
Special Courts/tribunals, Fast Track Courts, computerisation of courts, and 
adoption of alternative modes of dispute resolution, such as, arbitration and 
conciliation. Lok Adalats have been given a statutory base as supplementary 
forum for resolution of disputes.

Retrieval of Relics of Maharaja Ranjit Singh 
SHRI KARTAR SINGH DUGGAL (Nom inated): Sir, my Special 
Mention relates to retrieval of the relics of Maharaja Ranjit Singh. Year-long 
celebrations of the bi-centenary of Ma haraja Ranjit Singh's coronation on 12 th 
April, 1801 were inaugurated by the Prime Minister a few weeks ago. As the 
last bastion to hold out against the British, Ranjit Singh's kingdom was the last 
to lay arms. 
Ever since 2000 BC, with the influx of Aryans, every invasion on 
India had been from West to East. It wa s for the first time that an Indian ruler 
went westward, crossed the Indus River in 1826, hoisted his flag on Kabul 
Fort, and turned the tide for good. 
Now that the bi-centenary of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's coronation is 
being celebrated at All-India level, it will be a befitting tribute to the Maharaja if 
the Government initiates action to get back the Koh-i-Noor -now lying in the 
crown jewels at the tower of London, the golden throne of Maharaja Ranjit 
Singh - now lying in the Victoria & Albert Museum, the flag of Maharaja Ranjit 
Singh with the descendents of the Lord Dalhousie family

UK, under the orders of Lord Dalhousie, th e then Governor General of India,

birthday of Guru Gobind Singh was celebrated in 1996, the Government had

Plight of a new University abandoned by the State and the Centre 
DR. M.N. DAS (Orissa): Sir, I refer to a very unique situation in the 
sphere of higher education. The title of my Special Mention is "Plight of a new 
university abandoned both by the State an d the Centre. Sir, Orissa which is a 
major State of the Indian Union, with  near 4-crore population, has fewer 
universities compared to some other States. After decades of demand, the 
Orissa Government finally established a University at Vyasa Vihar, in 
Balasore, in July 1999, and named it after Vyasa Kabi Fakir Mohan Senapati 
who is acknowledged as the Father of modern Oriya prose literature. Under 
Section 2F of the UGC Act, 1956, this University was included in the list of 
Indian Universities. Unfortunately, due to financial constraints of the State 
Government, teaching departments were not established, and the University 
functions only as an affiliating University . In such a situation, the University 
Grants Commission does not provide gr ants under section 12B of the UGC 
Act, and the Central Government also does not come forward with financial 
assistance. 
The University was established with an objective to offer new 
courses like Master of Computer Applic ation, Master in Computer Science, 
Information Technology, Marine Biology, etc., besides postgraduate studies in 
Science and Humanities. The realisation of all such hopes appears remote on 
account of the non-availability of fin ancial assistance, both from the State and 
the University Grants Commission. 
A newly established and recognised University direly needs essential 
infrastructure in terms of land, buildings, laboratories, staff, library and many 
other basic requirements. Hopes of mi llions appear to be belied. Even after 
three years of the founding of the University, it suffers from total negligence. I 
appeal to the hon. Minister of Human Resource Development kindly to rescue 
the Fakir-Mohan University of  Orissa before it is too late. The Government of 
Orissa needs direction and guidance from the Centre in respect of qualitative 
response towards higher education.  Thank you. 
Starvation deaths in Orissa 
SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIKAR (Karnataka): Mr. Chairman, Sir, it was 
astonishing and agonising to hear the shoc king news of starvation deaths in a 
village of Kashipur district of Orissa. It is a matter of concern that news of 
starvation deaths is still pouring in, ev en after 54 years of independence. We 
had a lot of discussions on over-production of foodgrains, excess 
224 

[20 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA  
stocks of foodgrains in the godowns across the country and distribution of 
excess stocks through the public distribution system. After all these 
discussions and the follow-up actions by the Government, it is hurting that the 
Government could not prevent these deat hs. Is there something wrong in the 
mechanism set up to manage this situation? 
The Central Government blames the State Government for this type 
of lapses saying that distribution is th e responsibility of the State Government. 
But my question is: Is it not the responsibility of every Government, every 
individual, to help, at least, those who are dying of hunger? At a time when 
people are dying like a bunch of ants, it  is a pity that one Government is 
shifting the responsibility to the other. The core question is: Who should 
protect the citizens' right to live? T he local authorities say that they had 
supplied 2 kilograms of foodgrains to every family. Hundreds of tonnes of 
foodgrains become waste and perish du ring transition. Is it not the 
responsibility of the Govern ments, both at the Centre  and in the State, to 
supply these foodgrains-before they become unfit for. human consumption-
free of cost to these people who are li ving in the regions which are identified 
as the worst-affected areas by natural calamities, sometimes, by flood and, 
sometimes, by severe drought. 
Let me take this opportunity to bring to the notica of this august 
House that the expenditure on supply of free foodgrains in the districts like 
Kashipur across the country will not co me even to 10 per cent of the UTI 
scam or any other scams that we have experienced in recent times. 
Under the circumstances, I strongly urge the hon. Prime Minister to 
evolve a system by which the author ities, under the supervision of the 
Government, Central or State, should ho ld a minimum stock of foodgrains for 
supplying in those areas which are faci ng extremely critical situations, and 
they be empowered with some powers to identify and supply the foodgrains 
on the basis of post facto approval by Government, as the cost would be 
negligible as mentioned above.  Thank you.

Ration for poor 
SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA (Uttar Pradesh): Sir, the record number of 
deaths in Kashipur of Orissa and Nandur bar of Maharashtra due to starvation 
and malnutrition is a shameful thing fo r our nation. Actually, when an inquiry 
was conducted, it was found that foodgrains were diverted and they never 
reached the poor and the tribal for whom it was intended. The tribals were 
denied sugar and kerosene and they were given only half their quota of 
foodgrains. This apart, the owners of t he PDS shops confiscated their ration 
cards, and this fact was very much known to the district administration. All this 
happens when the foodgrains are rotting. Still worse is the level of the off-take 
of rice by the States where starvation deaths are taking place. The figures of 
allocation and off-take (in 'ooo tonnes) respectively in relation to various 
States are as follows: Chhatisgarh,  21.5 and 17.5; Gujarat, 16.9 and 6.1; 
Himachal Pradesh, 3.5 and 0.38; Mahar ashtra 45.8 and 19.9; Orissa, 65.9 
and 36.8 and Rajasthan, 0.44 and 0.0. The hon. Prime Minister had declared 
that "democracy and hunger cannot go together" and also after the starvation 
deaths in six States were reported, the Supreme Court gave a directive in July 
enjoining that "no person should go hungry when the granaries are full". 
These have remained on paper only. The district administrations are yet to 
show sensitiveness to human suffering. God will not forgive those indulging in 
corrupt and malpractices in the distri bution of foodgrains to the poor and the 
poorest of

Drought and Scarcity conditions being faced by State of Maharashtra 
SHRI R. S. GAVAI (Mahar ashtra): Sir, the Stat e of Maharashtra has 
been facing severe drought and scarcity conditions since the last six months. 
So far, the Maharashtra Government  has spent Rs. 1,200 crores on the 
employment guarantee scheme to provi de job to the agricultural labourers, to 
meet the scarcity of drinking water and the scarcity of fodder to the cattle. 
In many parts of the State, t he monsoon has come late and hence 
the kharif crop had to be re-sown by th e cultivators. Thus , the cultivators had 
to bear a great loss. Unfortunately, there is a long wait for rains in many parts 
of the State and this has affected the crop s very badly. Kharif crops are not jn 
a survival condition, and because of lack of rains, the cultiv ation of rabi crops 
is not possible. The situatio n in Maharashtra is very precarious. In many parts 
of the State, people are facing drinking water problem, lack of fodder for the 
cattle and unemployment of agricultural labourers. As mentioned earlier, the 
Government of Maharashtra has taken several steps to tackle the situation 
and it has already spent Rs. 1,200 cror es. Earlier, the Government of 
Maharashtra had approached the Central Government for rendering financial 
help to enable the Government to effectiv ely deal with the si tuation, but there 
has been no response from them. This shows the step-motheriy treatment 
being shown by the Central Government towards Maharashtra. Earlier, in this 
Session itself, there was a demand that  the Centre should release Rs.500 
crores to the Government of Maharashtra  to deal with the scarcity condition. I 
once again earnestly request the Central Government to provide the financial 
assistance of Rs.500 crores to the Government of Maharashtra.

SHRI SURESH A. KESWANI (Maharashtra): I thank you, Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, for giving me time to speak on this very important issue. The  
issue has arisen out of the Mid-term Ap praisal of the Ninth Plan, which has 
been forwarded to us. It is a document which has generated enormous amount 
of debate and a cause for serious rethinking on allocation of our Plan priorities, 
allocation of our resources, re-examination of our entire administrative 
mechanism, whether we are capable of  dealing with the issues which are 
before us, whether we are able to overcome  the obstacles that we are likely to 
face and how we are going to face the emerging situation. 
Sir, as our leader here, Pranab Da, has pointed out, one must 
concede that the Government has been  able to maintain stability of our 
exchange rate; there has been a relative control of the rate of inflation and there 
is also comfortable foreign exchange reserve position. There have also been 
miscellaneous plusses which have been mentioned by various speakers, and, 
therefore, I do not wish to consume my time on them. 
Sir, the issue that I would like to highlight here is what has been the 
achievement of our much-trumpeted, the so-called second generation of

reforms that this Government  presented. Today, the 20 th of August, one 
remebers our great, late, leader, Mr. Rajiv Gandhi, who ushered us into the 
information-age with a total revolutionised thinking. He produced technology 
missions, he created a scientific temper, he talked about a tomorrow, a 
promise of tomorrow, which all young people like us wanted to work for and 
bring for our future generations. Sir, t oday, what does the Mid-term Appraisal 
of the Ninth Plan say? There is a fall in  the growth rate of GDP, there is a 
significant drop in the growth performance of agriculture, mining, industry, and 
what notl There is a fall in domestic savings, there is a fall in investment. The 
investment in public sector has droppe d. There are serious leakages in the 
tax-revenue that we are collecting. The tax-GDP ratio is down from 10.4 per 
cent to 8.5 per cent. The budgetary suppor t to the Plan is, therefore, bound to 
drop. What will be the effect? The public investment is unlikely to reach the 
targetted figure. What are going to be the consequences? There is going to be 
a fall in output, there is going to be a fa ll in employment, there is going to be a 
fall in incomes, there is going to be a fall in investments, and all cumulatively 
will further push us down into a further economic downfall. Consequently, the 
public investment in physical and social in frastructure will also drop, thereby, 
further weakening the growth rate duri ng the Tenth Plan period. Why has this 
happened? What is the reason for this? We must examine that. This has 
happened because we have so quickly forgotten the twin objectives of the 
Government and the governance, which were enshrined by my late leader, 
Mrs. Indira Gandhi. What were those two objectives? The first objective was 
the eradication of poverty, and the second objective was playing our rightful 
role in the international arena. 
For instance, a family of 100 persons goes to live in a small village, 
which has a population of 500. Now, this hundred members become one-sixth 
of the total population of that village . Suppose half the members are weak, 
they will concentrate on these twin objectives. They will balance these two 
things. On the one hand, they will st rengthen the weak; they will feed the 
weak; they will make them capable of performing; on the other, they will not 
neglect their performance in the internat ional arena. What is the international 
arena? We have signed the GATT. We are one of the signatories to the 
GATT. We have certain obligations under the WTO. We were quite conscious 
of the fact ten years ago that we woul d have, in ten years time, a totally new 
environment where we would be having international trade at our doorsteps. 
What did we do? Did we prepare for that ?   Today, what is happening is that 
we are finding ourselves suddenly

need not really reel out the statistics. But I will just cite a few examples. 
If you see agriculture, the targeted growth in the Ninth Plan was 
3.9%. But we could achieve only 1.5%. In manufacturing, the targeted growth

where we have failed very badly. In this background, even the revised target

quarter, the direct taxes have fallen by 28% and indirect taxes by 7%. The 
revenue receipts, as a percentage of GDP, have fallen from 11.3% in 1989-90

Mukherjee, has said, any Government should be careful about its revenues 
because the revenues have to be deployed for creating assets. We can't just 
depend on borrowings for creating assets. Therefore, the Government has to 
take utmost care in seeing to it that the revenue is improved.

flow into the country is merely 2.2 b illion U.S. dollars, whereas China could 
attract 38 billion U.S. dollars. Many a speaker in this House has compared the 
economic situation of our country with that of China. When China is able to 
attract 38 billion U.S. dollars, why are we not able to attract more than 2.2 
billion U.S. dollars? If you see, for the last 20 years, China attracted 330 billion 
U.S. dollars, whereas India could attract only 18 billion

*404. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the 
Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Bangladesh has placed restrictions on the import of rice from 
India; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what action Government have taken to find alternate markets for the 
export of rice from West Bengal where the price of rice has fallen due to 
"warehouse clearance" for the arrival of new harvest? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid 
on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) No restriction has been imposed by the Government of 
Bangladesh on import of rice from India. The National Board of Revenue 
has however, issued an order that rice can be imported only 
18

through Benapole and not through other landports. There is no restriction on 
importing rice through seaports. In addition, the import duty on rice has been 
increased from 5% to 25% alongwith a 10% regulatory duty with effect from 
1.7.2001. 
(c) The Government has permitted export of 30 lakh MT of rice out of the 
stocks held by FCI for the Central Pool in the current financial year. Some of 
the other steps taken to increase the export of rice from India and find 
alternate markets include conducting publicity campaigns, sending 
delegations abroad, participating in International trade fairs, inviting potential 
buyers and providing financial assistance to exporters for improving quality, 
packaging, brand promotion of products and for conducting market surveys.

Assam Gas Cracker Project 
*405. SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN: DR. 
ARUN KUMAR SARMA: 
Will   the   Minister   of  PETROLEUM   AND   NATURAL   GAS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the    details    of    agreement    for    supply    of   gas    to    the 
proposed Gas Cracker Project in Assam; and 
26 

[21 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) whether there is any dispute as regards the agreement among the. 
parties, if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) and (b) 6.35 million standard cubic meters per day (MMSCMD) 
of gas supply is the estimated requirement for production of 2 lakh tonne per 
annum (TPA) of ethylene in the Assam Gas Cracker Project for which both 
Oil & Natural Gas Corporation Limited (ONGC) and Oil India Limited 
(OIL) are to supply gas. OIL has signed a Gas Supply Agreement (GSA) on 
October 19, 2000 with Reliance Assam Petrochemicals Limited (RAPL) for 
supply of 5.0 MMSCMD for the Assa m Gas Cracker Project. The salient 
features of the agreement are given below:— 
(i) The gas supplies by OIL will be 5.0 MMSCMD for 15 years at a 
concessional price of Rs. 600 per thousand standard cubic meters 
(SCM) exclusive, of royalty, duties, taxes, levies and transportation 
charges for gas after extracting Ethane and heavier fractions. 
(ii) RAPL will extract Ethane and ot her heavier components required for 
production of Ethylene from the gas supplied and will return lean gas 
to OIL. 
(iii) Government of India shall comp ensate OIL for concessional price of 
gas. 
(iv) OIL shall make up the shortfall, whether on account of quality or 
quantity, by supplying additional quantity of gas at the same 
concessional price. 
(v) RAPL shall pay for loss of calor ific value for return gas volume and 
shall also pay compensation on account of short upliftment of 
feedstock, while OIL will be liable to pay compensation for net gas 
short supplies. 
(vi) If additional gas is available with OIL after meeting its own 
requirements, OIL shall supply gas to RAPL to make up the short 
supply by ONGC only after they have supplied the gas not less than 
1.35 MMSCMD. 
(vii) The   agreement   provides   for   compliance   of   conditions

precedent set out in the agreement by the respective parties within 
18 months from the date of signing of the gas supply agreement. 
Such condition precedent can be waived by mutual consent or 
agreement. 
RAPL and ONGC are in the process of finalising gas supply agreement 
for supply of balance feedstock of 1.35 MMSCMD of the Assam Gas 
Cracker Project.

*407. SHRI SATISH PRADHAN: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Police has arrested the cashier of Memon Co-
operative Bank, Mumbai, for bringing into market fake currency notes of Rs. 
500/-; 
(b) whether this has any connection with drug mafia gang in which Director of 
the above Bank was arrested; 
(c) whether ISI is involved in this matter; and 
(d) what steps Government propose to take to stop such incidents? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) Yes, Sir. Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has 
reported that as per report received from the Memon Co-operative Bank Ltd., an 
Assistant Cashier-cum-Junior Clerk of the bank had been arrested by the Mumbai 
Police in June, 2001 for circulating fake currency notes of Rs. SOCK- (Rupees Five 
Hundred) denomination. 
(b) and (c) The matter is being investigated by Mumbai Police. 
(d) The Union Government has taken a number of steps to curb the 
circulation of fake currency notes which, inter-alia, include setting up a special unit 
in the Central Bureau of Investigation for exclusive investigation of counterfeit 
currency notes, scaling up vigilance by the Border Security Force/Custom 
Authorities to prevent smuggling of such currency notes into the c ountry, 
incorporation of special security features in higher denomination notes and 
dissemination of information on security features through print media and 
Doordarshan for benefit of public. Further, a High Level Technical Committee of 
Experts with representatives from Ministry of Home Affairs, National Security 
Council Secretariat, Reserve Bank of India and the Printing Presses has been 
constituted for examining the whole gamut of problem caused by circulation of 
fake currency notes.

         SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD:

markets?

          SHRI SUKHDEV SINGH LIBRA: 
Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of companies given licence to run mobile telephone services in

services (both incoming outgoing) calls are such higher in Punjab as compared to 
mobile services in other parts of the country;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) Sir, two private 
companies namely, M/s. Bharti Mobile Limited (earlier name M/s. J.T. Mobile 
Limited) and M/s. Spice Communications Limited alongwith Bharat Sanchar 
Nigam Limited (BSNL) were granted licence to operate Cellular Mobile

by the Service providers. The Standard Tariff Package offered by the CMTS 
providers is identical in all parts of the country including Punjab Telecom Circle. 
In addition to the standard package, the service providers are free to offer 
alternative tariff packages subject to approval of the TRAI. The subscriber is free

comprise different rates

area.

3113. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news 
item   captioned  "Opium  to  heroin   via  India ................. Indian   Chemical 
Afghan druglords can't do without" appearing in the Times of India dated the 
8th April, 2001 pointing out smuggling of a vital chemical needed to convert 
opium into heroin out of India and sold in Pakistan and Afghanistan; 
(b) if so, what is Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) the steps taken to check the reported smuggling activity? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Drug smuggling is a clandestine activity. While there have been 
seizures of Acetic Anhydride of I ndian origin in India as well as 
abroad, there is nothing to indicate that it is "systematically being 
smuggled out of the country and sold to drug lords in Pakistan and 
Afghanistan". 
(c) All cases of smuggling of Acetic Anhydride are actively 
investigated and action taken under the NDPS Act. Government has 
imposed stringent controls on Acetic Anhydride to check its 
smuggling and misue. Some of the steps taken in this regard are (i) 
declaring Acetic Anhydride as a 'Controlled Substance' under the 
NDPS Act which implies that all manufacturers, traders, importers, 
exporters and consumers of the chem ical are required  to maintain 
records and file returns with Narcotics Control Bureau as per the 
NDPS (Regulation of Controlled Substances) Order, 1993 and 
violation of the provision attracts imprisonment of up to ten years 
and fine; (ii) requirement of a No objection certificate from the 
narcotics Commissioner for the export/import of Acetic Anhydride 
out of India; (iii) Special checks on the movement of Acetic 
Anhydride under the Customs Act along the border with Myanmar 
and Pakistan; and (iv) the Indian enforcement agencies, Narcotics

Control Bureau (NCB) and Central Bureau of Narcotics (CBN) coordinate 
with other competent national authorities empowered to regulate or enforce

1988.

RBI's concern on sustainability of Government finances 
3119. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that in its monthly bulletin for July, 2001, the 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has expressed concern regarding the * 
sustainability of Government's finance; 
(b) if so, the areas identified as the major areas of concern; 
(c) whether Government share the sa me perception as the RBI with 
regard to this matter; and 
(d) if so, the steps proposed to be taken to ease the situation in these 
areas? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE-PATIL): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Reserve Bank of India has id entified the following major areas of 
concern  regarding stability  and sustainability  of Central - 
106 

[21 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
finances. First, the revenue base of the Centre continues to be weak with 
stagnation of revenue-GDP and tax-GDP ratios. Second, going by the past 
experience, any shortfall in the realisation of disinvestment receipts may put 
pressure on the fisc in achieving the fiscal deficit targets. Third, the gross 
market borrowings of the Centre have been persistently rising over the years. 
The larger recourse to borrowings to finance expenditure has contributed to 
downward rigidity in the debt-GDP ratio. 
(c) and (d) The long-term sustainability of the fiscal policy rests upon the 
complete elimination of revenue deficit and containment of fiscal deficit 
within a manageabel level. With a view to achieving fiscal consolidation, the 
Budget for 2001-02 emphasises expenditure management through the process 
of bringing about structural changes in the composition of Central 
Government expenditure, economy in non-plan revenue expenditure while 
improving the quality of expenditure. To this end the Budget contains a 
number of initiatives which among others include restricting fresh 
recruitment to one per cent of total civilian staff strength, user charges for 
services provided by the government and its agencies to be revised keeping in 
view the increased cost of these services etc. Further, with a view to reducing 
interest burden, most administered interest rates were reduced by 1.5 per cent 
as of March 1, 2001. Besides, the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget 
Management Bill, 2000 was introduced  in Parliament in December, 2000. 
This Bill includes provisions relating to ceilings on debt, deficit and 
borrowing.

†3190. SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH 'LALAN': 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a National Water Policy is required for power distribution 
and better management of water in the country; 
(b) if so, what is Government's reaction in this regard; 
(c) whether Government have made any concrete efforts during the last 
three years for preparing a water policy; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and by when water policy is expected to be 
formulated? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (d) 
National Water Policy (1987) provides for planning, development and 
management of water resources in the country. There is a separate policy on 
Hydro Power Development. The National Water Policy was adopted in 1987 
by the National Water Resources Council (NWRC) headed by the Prime 
Minister with all the Chief Minist ers of States and Chief Ministers-
Administrators of Union Territories as its members. This policy is presently 
under revision/updation based on the experiences of last 14 years and new 
issues/challenges emerged in water resources sector. The draft updated 
National Water Policy has been formulated and finalised by the National 
Water Board in 1998. The draft policy has also been considered by the 
National Water Resources Council in its 4th meeting held on 7th July, 2000 
under the Chairmanship of the Hon'bl e Prime Minister. The deliberations 
established a consensus among the States on most of the important issues 
contained in the proposed draft updated National Water Policy. However, 
some areas were found needing further more discussions.    In    order   to   
examine   and   for   achieving   greater 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
171 

RAJYA SABHA [21 August, 2001] 
convergence and agreement on these is sues as well, a Working Group of 
IrrigationAVater Resources Ministers of  all the States/ Union Territories 
under the Chairmanship of the Hon'ble Union Minister of Water Resources 
was constituted on 9th October, 2000. The first meeting of the Working 
Group was held on 22nd May, 2001 wherein the draft updated National

Water Management Schemes 
3199. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to give new thrust to the innovative 
Water Management Schemes to be implemented throughout the country in 
view of the recurring drought, floods and watershortage in cities like Delhi 
and Chennai; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) 
Recognizing the need for conservation and management of water resources, 
due emphasis for this has been laid in the National Water Policy - 1987. The 
policy provides various measures for better water management and 
conservation. However, water, being a State subject, it is primarily the 
responsibility of the concerned State Governments to plan, finance and 
execute schemes for development and management of water. The Central 
Government provides financial and technical support to them in this 
endeavour. In order to improve water availability and water quality the 
Central Government is promoting rain water harvesting through water shed 
management programme, artificial recharge of ground water and roof top 
rain water harvesting. The Central Ground Water Board is implementing a 
pilot Central Sector Scheme on "Studies on Artificial Recharge of Ground 
Water" with a view to assess the efficacy of various recharge structures in some 
'Over-exploited' and 'Dark' blocks of the country. The Government has 
earmarked an amount of Rs.25.00 crore during the IX Five Year Plan for the 
scheme. 
181 

RAJYA SABHA [21 August, 2001] 
The Ministries of Rural Devel opment and Agriculture are also 
implementing various programmes in the country having water conservation 
component. These programmes are:- 
1. National Watershed Development Project for Rainfed Areas 
(NWDPRA) 
2. Soil Conservation in the Catchment of River Valley Project. 
3. Integrated Watershed Management in the Catchment of Flood Prone 
Rivers (FPR) 
4. Watershed Development Project for Control of Shifting Cultivation 
Area (WDPSCA) in North-Eastern India. 
5. Drought Prone Area Programme (DPAP) 
6. Desert Development Programme (DDP) 
7. Integrated Wasteland Development Project (IWDP) 
With a view to promoting roof top rain water harvesting, the Ministry of 
Water Resources has proposed to the Ministry of Urban Development to 
consider enactment of suitable legislation for provision of roof top rain water 
harvesting in cities, Accordingly, the Madras Metropolitan Development 
Authority (MMDA) has issued regulations for conservation of roof top rain 
water. Delhi Government has also decided to make water harvesting 
compulsory in all new residential buildings, group housing societies and 
plotted residential areas of over 500 sq. mts.

RE. QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL (Bihar): Mr. Chairman, with your permission, 
under rule 188 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the 
Council of States, I wish to raise a question of privilege in respect of a 
specific matter of recent occurrence wh ich requires the intervention of the 
Council. The question of privilege relates to the Finance Minister, Shri 
Yashwant Sinha, who, during the course of his response in the Rajya Sabha, 
in the Short Duration discussion relating to the UTI, misled the House by, 
inter alia, stating the following on August 1, 2001, "If we had been kept in 
the picture, if he had come to us, we would have told him as to what exactly 
had to be done. After all, if we can solve the problem after the 2 nd of July, 
why could we not have solved the problem before 2nd July. It was not because 
of any lack of desire or will on the part of the Ministry of Finance. It was 
entirely because, deliberately, we were kept in the dark..."He further says 
"...Secondly, on what strength does the Ministry of Finance interfere at that 
stage and ask the UTI to do one and no t do the other? We, therefore, decided 
it may be an error judgment, I do not know, but, at that point of time, that was 
the judgment that we made in the Ministry of Finance -- to intervene only 
after the UTI Board had taken a decision; we intervened only after the UTI 
Board took the decision in its wisdom."

SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIKAR (Karnataka): Respected Madam, first 
of all, I want to thank you for the opportunity that you have given me to 
speak on this Bill. The proposed amendment is to increase the borrowing 
capacity of the Food Corporation of India and this deserves the support of the 
House. But, keeping this- in view, I would like to say, at present, all the 
godowns are filled with grains and the Government is not in a position to buy 
more foodgrains from the farmers. Because of this, th e condition of the 
farmers became very critical. The result is: The farmers started committing 
suicides. This is due to fall in the prices of foodgrains. This is the condition of 
our farmers. Now, the Government is taking full care about it and we all 
know about it. Our first and the foremost duty is to protect our farmers. Being 
a Member of the Standing Committee on Food and Civil Supplies, I had an 
opportunity to visit some of the godowns. We had seen the condition of the 
godowns. The godowns are full of grains. There is no place  to  store  
foodgrains  properly.     We  all   know  about   the  climatic

conditions. There were heavy rains and there were sudden climatic changes 
in our country. The foodgrains are also stocked in a verandah The foodgrains 
are being dumped in bags. There is no  proper storage facility. The condition 
of godowns is such that even the medicines which are used to prevent the 
foodgrains from getting deteriorated, cannot be put. When we went for 
inspection, we were told that, every m onth, they put medicines and all that. 
But the godowns are full to such an extent that whosoever wants to put the 
medicines, can only put them around the bags. The situation is such that 
nobody can do anything. They cannot ev en lift the bags; they can't even put 
the medicines. As they cannot put the medicines, a large quantity of 
foodgrains is deteriorating. All this is happening because of the lack of 
storage facilities. Whenever we go there, they make a complaint that 
godowns are not available; and, th e godowns which are available are 
completely full. They even tried to take some godowns on hire basis, but that 
was not possible. Therefore, I would lik e to say that what ever foodgrains are 
available, the Government should take proper care of that. It can send those 
foodgrains to the States where people are dying of hunger. When we ask the 
States, they say 'we are not getting the foodgrains'; and, when we ask the 
Central Government, it says,"the State Governments are not lifting the 
foodgrains." This way, one Government is putting the blame on the other 
Government. As a result, the foodgrains are deteriorating. During the 
discussion, they even expressed the vi ew that they wanted to export the 
foodgrains because they were not getting proper rates here. The Government 
should not think about the rates; it should not think about exporting the 
foodgrains. In some States, the people are dying of hunger. For example, in 
Orissa, 25 people died because there was no food. So, the Government 
should send these foodgrains to such areas either at a low price or free so that 
the lives of the people, who are dying of hunger, could be saved.

the godowns which are full of grains and then purchase foodgrains to be put

SHRI CO. POULOSE (Kerala): Madam Deputy Chairman, the Food 
Corporations (Amendment) Bill, 2001  is a very simple Bill. But the 
amendment is important, in the present day context. The aim of the Bill is to 
remove the limitation of borrowing by the FCI. This is required by the FCI 
for procurement and for stock holding. The stock is increasing day by day. 
The offtake is very low. It has been reported that around 60 million tonnes of 
foodgrains is with the Food Corporation of India. It costs round about 
Rs.58,000 crores. The arbitrary decision of the Government to distinguish

between the BPL and the APL has kept around 75 per cent of the population 
out of the purview of the Public Distribution System. They have to purchase 
foodgrains from the PDS 'a t the economic price". Acco rding to the FCI, the 
economic cost is calculated taking in to account differen t factors. The 
economic cost, in almost all the cases, is above the prevailing market price. 
Nobody is willing to purchase at a high er price from the PDS. The economic 
cost is calculated by adding all other costs, incurred by the FCI like the cost 
of procurement, the cost of transport, the loss incurred during transportation 
and storage, interest cost and godown cost. This is how every is added. When 
everything is added, naturally, the economic price is always above the market

at the BPL definition, around Rs.49.06 for the rural population and around 
Rs. 56 for the urban population, as the boundary level for the BPL, is 
calculated, based on 1973-74 price level.

public distribution system at an increased price. So, they are compelled to 
purchase wheat and the other foodgrains needed, from the open market.

the Government is trying hard to get away the stocks from the godowns. The 
Government has increased the quota of  foodgrains for the BPL it was ten

foodgrains free of cost to the drough t-prone areas; there is open market sale

open market in other ways; there are also  attempts to export foodgrains at 
lower prices. By all these methods, the Government is trying its level best to 
reduce the stock. But the stock is not reducing. The stock is increasing day by 
day. What is the problem? The point is that the procure foodgrains from the 
peasants of this country should be prop erly, evenly and uniformly distributed

name of giving up subsidies, has made a diversion and that has created a 
dilemma for the Food Corporation of India. That is the problem the FCI is

other House, the Government is trying to grant loans to the SAARC countries 
to get away the wheat we are holding today.

SHRI S. VIDUTHALAI VIRUMBI (Tamil Nadu): Madam, the Bill 
which has been brought before us for discussion would enable the Food 
Corporation of India to  increase its borrowing capacity. Before this 
Amendment, the Food Corporation of India could avail loan from the 
financial institutions as well as banks to the tune of ten times the paid- up 
capital and the reserve fund. But, practically, there was no reserve fund with 
the FCI. Section 27 (b) says, "Issue and sell bonds and debentures carrying 
interest at such rates as may be fixed by the Central Government at the time 
the bonds or debentures are issued". Now after this Amendment, clause (b) 
alone will enable them to borrow 10 times the paid-up capital. By amending 
Section 27 of the Act, the clutches ar e being removed from this particular 
stipulation. So far as overdraft is concerned, in 1999-2000, the FCI borrowed 
Rs. 15,985 crores from the banks. In 2000-01, the FCI borrowed Rs. 25,167 
crores. The sanctioned amount was Rs. 1,480 crores. It is expected that in 
2001-02, they would require more than Rs. 30,000 crores. Before this 
Amendment, the FCI could overdraw to the tune of only Rs. 22,850 crores. 
This Amendment is essential because the foodgrain stock held by the FCI has 
been increasing year after year. On 1* ' January, 1999, the FCI had a stock of 
24.38 million tonnes.   On 1.1.2000,

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
External Affairs Minister's recent Visit to Nepal 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS AND THE MINISTER 
OF DEFENCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): Madam, I wish to inform the 
hon. Members that I made a goodwill visit to Nepal from August 17 to 19. 
The purpose of my visit was to personally convey to His Majesty 
King Gyanendra Bir Bikram Shah De v the deepest condolences of the 
President, the Prime Minister, the Government, and the people of India at the 
grievous tragedy that had struck Nepal in June. I also conveyed to His 
Majesty the good wishes of the President and the Prime Minister. 
249 

RAJYA SABHA [21 August. 2001] 
This visit was undertaken also to convey to the newly elected 
Prime   Minister   of   Nepal,   His   Excellency   Shri   Sher   Bahadur Deuba 
reaffirmation  of  India's  commitment  to  building  further  on  the existing 
friendship and cooperation between India and Nepal. 
I took the opportunity of the visit to meet with the President of the 
Nepali Congress, Shri Girija Prasad Koir ala, Leader of the Opposition, Shri 
Madhav Kumar Nepal, the President of the Nepal Sadbhavna Party, Shri 
Gajendra Narayan Singh, the President of the Rashtriya Pr ajatantra Party, 
Shri Surya Bahadur Thapa as also seni or statesmen, Shri Krishna Prasad 
Bhattarai. 
While my visit was essentially for the purpose of conveying 
goodwill, and for reaffirming India's commitment to our traditional ties of 
friendship and cooperation, issues of in terest to the two countries were also 
discussed. Some apprehensions had been voiced, in the media in Nepal, about 
the renewal of the existing Trade Treaty between our two countries. I 
conveyed that India remains fully committed to the growth of industry, in 
Nepal, enhancing trade between the two countries, also of growth of 
employment in Nepal. There were, howeve r, certain issues that had emerged 
during the implementation of the Treaty over the past five years, which now 
need to be addressed, then discussed between the two countries, and 
necessary adjustments made. I expresse d confidence that in the forthcoming 
discussions between the technical delegations of the two sides this would be 
resolved to mutual satisfaction. There had also been concerns expressed in 
Nepal about the possibility of adverse consequences, of a minor flood control 
embankment being constructed in district Siddhartha Nagar, of Uttar Pradesh. 
I conveyed that though technical provision had been made in this 
embankment for water to flow through 12 Regulators, and that there was 
unlikely to be any adverse impact, yet construction was promptly halted after 
the concerns of His Majesty's Governme nt were received by us. Since then, 
technical officials have met at site and will meet again. About apprehensions 
that this embankment might cause damage to Lumbini, I affirmed that these 
were totally unfounded. Lumbini is as sacred to India as it is to Nepal. 
I reiterated our willingness to jointly develop the water resources of 
Nepal so that Nepal becomes an energy  exporting country. The leadership of 
Nepal assured me of their desire also to make progress in this field. 
250 

[21 August. 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
I conveyed the Government of India's appreciation of the movement 
towards dialogue on the Maoist question and hoped that this would reach a 
successful conclusion. 
Our continuing concerns with re gard to the clandestine use of 
Nepal's territory for anti-Indian activities by the Pakistan ISI were also 
conveyed. I received a firm assurance from His Majesty's Government that 
any such activity against India would not be tolerated and that necessary 
steps would be taken. 
My exchange of views with political leaders in Nepal was most 
fruitful, constructive and forward looking. I found unanimity that the ties of 
friendship and cooperation between our two countries should continuously be 
strengthened, in a spirit of friendship, for the benefit of the peoples of Nepal 
and India. 
I am happy to report to the hon. Members that relationship between

†*421. SHRI SHYAM LAL: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any scheme for the construction and safety 
of reservoirs (ponds and lakes) of rural areas in order to contain the declining 
water level; and 
(b) if so, since when and if not, reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA): (a) and (b) A Statement 
is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
In order to contain the declining water levels, the construction and 
restoration of village ponds and other water harvesting structures, like percolation 
tanks and check dams are important activities envisaged in the three major 
Watershed Development Programmes, namely the Drought Prone Areas 
Programme (DPAP), the Desert Development Programme (DDP) and the 
Intergrated Wasteland Development Programme (IWDP) of the Department of 
Land Resources of the Ministry of Ru ral Development. Desiltation of village 
ponds and tanks is also covered under the Employment Assurance Scheme and 
the three Programmes mentioned above. In addition, the Rajiv Gandhi National 
Drinking Water Mission of the Ministry of Rural Development Provides funds 
under the Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP) and the Pradhan 
Mantri Gramodaya Yojana (Drinking Water Supply Component) for sustainability 
of sources, including rainwater harvesting. 
Activities to contain declining water levels are also taken up under the 
Watershed Development Programmes implemented by, amongst others, the 
Ministry of Agriculture and the Ministry of Environment & Forests. The Central 
Ground Water Board (of the Ministry of Water Resources) is implementing a 
Pilot Central Sector Scheme on the studies of "Ground Water Recharge" which 
has a component of rain water harvesting. Under this scheme, recharge through

Old Age Pensions are being provided in all State and Union Territories 
under the National Old Age Pension Scheme (NOAPS), administered by the 
Ministry of Rural Development whereby an amount of Rs. ISI- par month is 
made available to old and destitute persons aged 65 years and above. In addition, 
several State Governments and Union Territory Administrations provide old 
age pensions from their respective Budgets.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b)on 25.06.2001, about 15 Upper-caste people threatened the Dalits of 
Khuinbadi village in Junagarh district of Gujarat to vacate the waste-land 
occupied by the Dalits. An offence was registered against them by the Vanthli 
Police Station under sections 143,506(2) of the IPC and under section 3(1 )(10) 
of the SC/ST Prevention of Atrocitie s Act, 1989. All the accused were 
asrressted and sent to judicial cust ody. Necessary police bandobast was 
maintained to protect the Dalits and their property in the village. Meanwhile, 
about 20 Dalit families sat on a fast from 26.6.2001 to 31.7.2001 in front of the 
District Collector's Office to regulari ze the waste-land occupied by them. A 
meeting was held on 31.7.2001 by the Collector Junagarh in his office in

month and the sufficient police bandobast would be provided to the Harijans

both the communities participated alongw ith their local leaders. Members of 
the district administration were also present on the occasion. Subsequently 
there has been no tension irvthe village. However, police bandobast and vigil 
continue in the village. 
(c) 'Public order' and 'Police' ar e State subjects as per the Seventh 
Schedule to the Constitution of India. The registration, investigation, 
detection and prevention of crimes ar e primarily the responsibility of the 
State Governments. However, the Government of India has been advising the 
Staie Governments, from time to time, to give more focussed attention to 
improving administration of criminal justice system to ensure prevention of 
atrocities against Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, women and other 
vulnerable sections of the society. The advisories issued by the Government
