Swaranjayanti Gram Swarojgar Yojana 
*435. SHRI K.M. SAIFULLAH: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Ministry has stressed the need for making the self-help groups 
a national movement through the medium of Swaranjayanti Gram Swarojgar 
Yojana to help in the development of social sector; 
(b) if so, whether Government have decided to carry out necessary 
modifications in the guidelines for the SGSY; and 
(c) if so, to what extent these measures have improved the development of 
the social sector in rural areas? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M. VENKAIAH 
NAIDU: (a to c) The Self-Help Group (SHG) approach being followed under 
the Swaranjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) envisages organisation of 
me rural poor and their training and capacity building through a process of 
social mobilisation. The group approach provides an opportunity to the rural 
poor to come together on a common platform, discuss social and economic 
issues relevant to them and arrive at collective decisions aimed at their overall 
betterment. 
At the National Conference on the 'SHG Movement in the country and 
the SGSY' held recently at the Natio nal Institute of Rural Development 
(NTRD), Hyderabad, it was, in pursuance of the empowering effect of the 
Group approach on members of SHGs, unanimously resolved to develop the 
Self Help Groups as a National Movement and to form at least one such 
Group in all habitations of the country by the year 2004. 
In the context of the issues ra ised at the National Conference, 
appropriate modifi cations in the SGSY Guidelines are presently being 
processed for early implementation.

3268. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: W ill the Minister of POWER be

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) The Energy Review Committee 
headed by Dr. Madhav Godbole was constituted by the Government of 
Maharashtra. The Committee has submitted its second report to the Government 
of Maharashtra on 11th July, 2001. The second report makes several 
recommendations regarding reform of the Maharashtra power sector. The 
recommendations in brief are as follows: 
* Distribution regions should not be escrowed prior to privatisation. 
* Government of Maharashtra should build consensus around its 
restructuring strategy. 
* The report of the Committee should be published for information of the 
people as soon as possible. 
97 

RAJYA SABHA [22 August, 2001] 
* Implementation of the 'Maharashtra reform Model' evolved by the 
Committee (unbundling of Maharashtra State Electricity Board (MSEB) 
into separate generation companies, transmission company and distribution 
business). 
* Progressive privatisation of distribution. 
* Hydro generation stations and Urban plant should be corporatised as a 
single state owned entity, i.e. Maharashtra Power Corporation Ltd (MPCL). 
* Transmission and system coordination services to remain under state 
ownership.  
* Distribution companies should be configured on basis of "concentrated 
zones". This would eliminate scope of cross-subsidy. 
* Second phase of reforms should start with progressive privatisation of 
distribution companies. 
* Pre-dominant non-urban distribution companies should initially remain 
under state ownership. 
* Sale of distribution business and generating companies through 
competitive bidding. 
* Generating companies except for MPCL should progressively be privatised 
after stabilization of the distribution companies. 
* Establishment of a Power Sector Reform Fund. 
* As a preparatory step towards the establishment of a bulk market, the 
Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (MERC) may consider 
regulating generation through a regulated cost-based pool, from which 
the distribution companies can source their power requirements. 
* Government of Maharashtra should take steps to vest the MERC with 
additional powers and increase its financial autonomy. 
* MERC to consider multi-year regul ation as it reduces not only the 
regulatory uncertainty but also the regulatory burden and also improves 
its quality of regulation by staggering the process of tariff application 
from different distribution companies. 
98 

[22 August,  2001] RAJYA  SABHA 
* In order to enable MERC to fulfill its role effectively, various functions 
listed under Section 22(2) of the Electricity Regulatory Commission's 
Act, 1998, which include regulation of investment approval and the 
operation of the power system and issuing of licenses, be entrusted to 
MERC with immediate effect. 
* MSEB to improve the information base so as to provide the MERC with a 
sufficient basis for embarking on a multi-year regulatory approach. 
* MSEB to undertake action to improve its performance to the extent possible 
(reallocation of employees, reduction of commercial payables, regularization 
of unauthorized connections). 
* Suitable laws to be enacted to give MSEB/Government of Maharashtra 
powers to penalize the guilty. MSEB to get a study commissioned to 
determine the energy and peak demand for the next five years. 
Any initiative based on the Committee's report is to be taken by the 
Government of Maharashtra.

(b) In 1972, Tehri Dam Project (600MW) was initially approved as a State 
Sector Project to be implemented by Government of U.P. at an estimated cost of 
Rs. 197.92 crores. The capacity of the Project was enhanced to 1000 MW in 1983. 
However, in view of the resource constraints faced by the State Government and 
keeping in view the requirement of power in the Northern Region of the country, 
it was decided in November, 1986 to implement the Tehri Dam Complex comprising 
(i) Tehri Dam and Hydro Electric Project (HEP) Stage-I (1000 MW), (ii) Koteshwar 
Dam and Power Project (400 MW) and (iii) Tehri Pump Storage Plan (PSP) (1000 
MW) as a joint venture of Government of India and the Government of Uttar 
Pradesh. These projects are being executed through the Tehri Hydro Development 
Corporation (THDC). 
In March, 1994, approval was accorded to the Tehri Hydro Development 
Corporation for implementing the Tehri Dam and HEP Stage-I (1000 MW) at an 
estimated cost of Rs. 3391.40 (March, 1993 Price Level) including IDC of Rs. 
427.74 crores. The cost estimates included the committed works of Koteshwar 
HEP and essential works of Tehri PSP. 
The revised cost estimates of the Tehri HEP Stage-I (1000 MW) including 
essential works of Tehri PSP are Rs. 5690.64 Crores (August 1999 Price Level) 
including IDC and financial charges. The increase in the cost, apart from normal 
escalation, has been due to various factors including design changes to ensure 
safety of the Dam in the context of the seismicity of the region, additional measures 
for rehabilitation of project affected families based on the recommendations of 
Hanumantha Rao Committees, availing of specialized consultancy services, foreign 
exchange variation and variation in statutory duties and levies, etc.

JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) An accident took place in Cooling Tower No. 
1 at Simhadri Thermal Power Project of the National Thermal Power Corporation 
(NTPC) on 28th March, 2001. The construction work of Cooling Tower is being 
executed by M/s National Building Construction Corporation (NBCC), a 
Government of India Undertaking, under a turnkey contract. The temporary access 
to facilitate transport of material was made of scaffolding pipes to the height of 165 
meters. This temporary access scaffolding collapsed at about 10.30 PM on 28th

Committee feels that the cumulative f actors like accidental jamming of the 
concrete bucket with the structure resulting in loosening of some couplers 
and loss of some members, possible loosening of some of the couplers of the 
scaffolding contributed to the accident and that the responsibility lies with 
M/s NBCC. The Committee suggested various recommendations to M/s NBCC 
to prevent recurrence of similar accident.

accident has been paid by M/s NBCC. Besides, statutory payment of about Rs.

Union Power Minister to have conditions of additional comfort and security 
being insisted upon by financial institutions from independent producers waived

regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to  (d) With a view to identify an acceptable 
payment security mechanism for Independent Power Producers (IPPs), in the 
eighth meeting of the Crisis Resolution Group (CRF) held on March 30, 
2000 under the chairmanship of Minister of Power, various alternatives to 
escrow were discussed. In this meeting, it was decided that financing of IPPs 
should be linked with the progress of reforms undertaken by the State 
Government. To facilitate private power projects to achieve financial closure, 
the Ministry of Power has proposed a reform based security mechanism as an 
alternative to escrow to provide financial comfort to the lenders and IPP 
promoters. The Financial Institutions have agreed to undertake financing of

Governments to provide escrow before commercial Operation Date instead

of this decision, a draft Memorandum  of Agreement (MoA) was prepared.

a total capacity of 2239 MW, has been initialed by the Government of Andhra 
Pradesh/APTRANSCO, Power Finance Corporation and the Financial 
Institutions led by Industrial Development Bank of India on August, 10,2001.

account 30 days before Commercial Operation Date instead of the present

Acute problem of potable drinking water in Saurashtra 
3294. PROF. (SHRIMATI) BHARATI RAY: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the whole of Saurashtra is facing an acute 
problem of potable drinking water for the third consecutive year; 
(b) if so, what immediate steps are being taken in this regard; and 
(c) what measures are being taken to solve the problem on a permanent 
basis? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA): (a) As reported by 
the Government of Gujarat, Saurashtra Region of the State was under the grip 
of acute shortage of water for two consecutive years, i.e. 1999-2000 and 
2000-2001. During the current monsoo n, the State has been receiving 
satisfactory rainfall. The pr esent storage in Saurashtra Reservoirs is 36% of 
the designed capacity and as the current monsoon is still on, it is expected 
that these reservoirs will be further replenished. However, reservoir supplying 
water to cities like Jamnagar and Rajkot, as on date, are not adequately 
replenished and need more inflow of water to sustain supplies to these up to 
next monsoon. 
(b) and (c) As reported by the Government of Gujarat, the State 
Government has implemented a bulk water pipeline project for transfer of Mahi/ 
Narmada water from Central and South Gujarat to Saurashtra for meeting the 
needs of drinking water supply to the districts of Amreli, Bhavnagar, parts of 
Rajkot and Junagadh. Towns and cities in Saurashtra region have been 
supplied water during the scarcity period. Drinking water works relating to 
distribution network are going on in Bhavnagar and Amreli districts at a total 
cost of Rs. 450 crore. Government of Gujarat has also sanctioned a project at 
an estimated cost of Rs. 1106 crore for supplying Narmada water drawn from 
Maliya Branch to the districts of Ja mnagar and Kachchh. The project is 
planned to be completed by December, 2002. These projects are part of the 
major drinking water supply projects based on the Sardar Sarovar Canal as 
source to cover 8215 villages and 195 towns of Saurashatra and Kachchh.

expenditure is the Calamity Relief Fund (CRF) for which 75% share is contributed 
by the Central Government. For major calamities, where funds in the CRF do not 
suffice, assistance is admissible from the National Calamity Contingency Fund 
(NCCF). These arrangements are in accordance with the award of the Eleventh 
Finance Commission (EFC). Apart from releasing the entire Central share of CRF

subject. Government of India supplements the efforts of the State by providing 
financial assistance under the Acceler ated Rural Water Supply Programme

Agriculture Crops Insurance Scheme 
SHRI R. KAMARAJ (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I wish to raise the matter 
regarding assessment of loss or damage to standing crops during natural 
calamities like floods and drought. Under the present Crop Insurance Scheme, 
"Harvest Tests' for assessing the loss or  damage to crops are being made by 
one or two survey members of one or two villages in a Taluk. They take the 
earlier year's production into considera tion. The difference in production of 
the previous year and the year in wh ich the crops are affected by natural 
calamities, is assessed. Accordingly,  compensation is paid to farmers. 
Because of this practice adopted for pu rposes of the Crop Insurance Scheme, 
farmers are unable to get the exact compensation for their loss. This method 
of loss assessment is not beneficial to farmers in getting compensation. The 
"Harvest Test' should be done by insurance people in all the villages which 
are affected by natural calamities, or, in, at least, fifty per cent of the affected 
villages so that the actual loss to farmers comes to light. Thereafter, an 
average of the loss or damage may be taken into consideration for purposes of 
compensation. 
I, therefore, request the Government to take necessary action for 
making suitable modifications in the existing method of assessment of loss or 
damage to crops in order to help farmers in getting a reasonable 
compensation.

GOVERNMENT BILLS 
THE MARRIAGE LAWS (AMENDMENT) BILL, 2001 
SHRIMATI SHABANA AZMI (Nominat ed): Sir, I rise to support 
the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2001. It is a matter of great shame that 
54 years after Independence, the women in our country face severe 
discrimination since their birth. In fact, they are not even allowed to be bom. 
The latest Census figures indicate that, in the age group of 0-6, the 
200 
 

[22 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
 
number of girls is less, compared to the boys. Alarmingly, it has gone down. 
It should be a matter of concern to all right-minded individuals. Girls are 
discriminated against and they are also denied equal access to food, nutrition, 
health, education and em ployment. Consequently, they end up by being 
totally dependent on either their father or their brother and later on their 
husbands. Alongwith this, the mind-set that exists is, the parents think that 
their primary duty -- in fact, their only duty- towards their daughter is to get 
her married off and then wash their hands off.   
यह माना जाता है िक िजस घर मȂ 
लड़की की डोली जाती है उस घर से िसफर्  उसकी अथीर् वापस आनी चािहए । Alongwith 
this, the constant pressure from all sections of the society to keep the 
marriage alive, under all circumstances , makes it almost impossible for the 
girl to leave an abusive home. There have been instances when a girl has 
gone back to her parents and has said, "my husband beats me", and the 
parents instead of saying, "this should not be allowed" have actually said 
"पित ही तो है , एकाध थÃपड़ मार िदया तो क्या" and sent her back to that abusive 
home. Such is the situation; which is why the women have to tolerate the 
abusive relations in our society. Sir, filing for divorce is an almost impossible 
exercise, because, firstly, it is a trauma tising experience, and, secondly, there 
is a great drain on the financial resources. She has absolutely no State 
support. If she goes back to her parents' home, she seriously jeopardises the 
chances of her younger sister getting married. She has no income of her own. 
And, so, it becomes an almost impossible exercise. 
Under these circumstances, one welcomes the Marriage Laws 
(Amendment) Bill, 2001. But, Sir, on cl osest scrutiny, one finds that the Bill 
seems to have a singular objective of introducing a 'time cap of 60 days' from 
the date of receipt of notice, on interim applicants for: 
 Alimony and expenses or litigation (Section 36 of the Indian Divorce 
Act, 1869). 
 Expenses on the suit, weekly or monthly pendente life maintenance 
(Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955; Section 49 of the Parsi 
Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936; and Section 36 of the Special Marriage 
Act, 1954). 
 Maintenance and education of children (Section 26 of the Hindu 
Marriage Act, 1955; Section 39 of th e Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 
1936; and Section 38 of the Special Marriage Act, 1954). 
201 

RAJYA SABHA [22 August, 2001] 
Now, often, these applications fail on account of the term 'income' 
of the husband being vaguely defined. Very often, the husbands pass of their 
life-style maintenance on to the comp any. That is why it is extremely 
important that the law should enable the Court to make sure that the lifestyle 
of the husband is also included; never mind if he pays for it or his company 
pays for it.   Therefore, the following amendment is suggested: 
"Provided that any application shall not be determined merely on the 
basis of income tax returns or any statement produced by the 
respondent. The court shall take into account the life-style of the 
respondent as evident from his expenditure on food, clothing, 
entertainment, housing, personal items and travel, irrespective of 
whether such expenditure is incurred or borne by the respondent in 
person or incurred or borne by any other person or company." 
Then, there should also be an easy way of recovering the amount of 
maintenance that is ordered. Accordingly, the law should empower the court 
to direct the employer to deduct from the husband's salary and pay directly to 
the wife. And, a similar provision may also be made in the case of debtors. 
The following amendment is accordingly suggested : 
"Where the Court is of the opinion that it is in the interest of justice, 
notwithstanding anything in any law in force, it may, by an order, 
direct the employer of the respondent or his debtor, to deduct the 
amount of monthly allowance of maintenance or expenses payable 
from his salary or debt and to directly pay the same to applicant." 
Sir, often, it becomes difficult to get the Respondent to disclose his 
assets. Also, often, the woman has to continue with the litigation without any 
money. Therefore, it is suggested that the Respondent be compelled to make a 
disclosure of assets, and make self-assessment of his liability (for a period of 
sixty days, i.e., until the interim appli cation can be decided), which amount 
has to be deposited with the court for disbursal to the applicant. The 
following amendment is suggested : 
"A person receiving notice of such an application shall be required to 
submit a self-assessment of his means and a computation of what 
would be his liability as maintenance expenses payable for a period 
of sixty days along with his reply to the Magistrate and shall deposit 
with the Magistrate the amount so computed for disbursal to the 
applicant.   An allowance under this section shall be payable 
202 

[22 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
from the date of the order, or, if so ordered, from the date of the 
application." 
Sir, along with it, Section 25(3) of the Hindu Marriage Act 
stipulates that maintaining "chastity" is essential to continue to enjoy the 
right to maintenance. This provision is moralistic and archaic and is often 
used to harass and embarrass lady litigants. It is recommended that this 
provision be deleted. 
Now, Sir, Section 27 of the Hind u Marriage Act enables the Court 
to make provisions for the disposal of joint property. However, property 
acquired during the subsistence of the ma rriage, in the name of either spouse 
and all household goods acquired during the marriage, are not covered by 
this section. This section should be amended to enable the court to allocate 
all such property in an equitable manner to either party, on the dissolution of 
the marriage. This will enable the court to take into consideration the 
contributions made by the woman to build up her matrimonial assets. 
In conclusion, while supporting the Marriage Laws (Amendment) 
Bill, 2001, I wish to reiterate that suitable laws such as the Domestic 
Violence Bill need to be implemente d to reduce the domestic violence and 
harassment of women. 
Sir, the Christian community, by itself, has asked for amendment in 
the Christian law. It is not being imposed from outside. That Bill is lying 
before a Standing Committee of Parliament. I demand that it should be 
brought for discussion and passed by the House as soon as possible. 
THE MINISTER OF LAW JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
AND MINISTER OF SHIPPING (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY) : We are passing 
it today itself. 
SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA (Tamil Nadu) : Sir, I welcome the 
Marriage Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2001. It is a good measure to help reduce 
the sufferings of the affected women. Si r, our leader, Dr. Puratchi Thalaivi, 
has made various programmes for the upliftment of women in the State. I am 
a practising advocate. I have some suggestions to make on the Amendment 
Bill. 
Sir, there is a clause which specifies that the alimony petition filed 
by the petitioner i.e. the wife, should be disposed of within 60 days.   But, in 
203 

RAJYA SABHA [22 August, 2001] 
the amendment Bill, there is no specific clause in regard to recovery of the 
money. After the order of the Magistrate is passed, if the husband fails to pay 
the maintenance amount, the petitioner has to again go to the court for the 
recovery of the money. That means, she has to file another petition or case or 
suite before the Civil Court. That will also take so many years to be disposed 
of. In the proposed amendment Bill, there is no specific mention about the 
recovery of money from the husband. Therefore, I would request the hon. 
Minister to make the necessary amendm ent in the parent law i.e. the Civil 
Procedure Code.

section of the society, which, after a broken marriage, is actually pushed into

large number of these matrimonial disputes have been pending in courts all 
over the country. There are two, three courts in every district of the country, 
which are only dealing with these issues.

resources, either for themselves or even for children, who were dependent 
upon them. So, the limited object of this law is that, in all such cases, we must 
endeavour to ensure by a legislative mandate that the courts must endeavour 
to show that within sixty days of the application being moved, the alimony 
question can be decided. We have also made laws more or less very similar.

fund for the benefit of advo cates and for mattersconnected 
therewith or incidental thereto, as passed by the Lok Sabha, 
be taken into consideration*. 
Madam, I will just explain the need for a Bill of this kind and what 
the salient features of this Bill are. It had been a longstanding demand of the 
lawyers all over the country that a Central legislation of this kind should be 
drafted. There are several State G overnments and State Assemblies which 
have already a law of this kind in pl ace and we had different experiences of a 
law of that kind. This law protects each one of them, unless those State 
Assemblies or the State Governments decide that they may find this as a 
beneficial provision and decide to transf er themselves and their lawyers into 
the benefits of this Bill. 
The scheme of this Bill is that it bears in mind that professionals 
otherwise do not have any element of social security. There is i .0 Provident 
Fund. There is no gratuity. There is no pension. Some of them, of course, do 
earn very well. But the earnings of a very large number of them are not so 
high as to even sustain them or their families out of the savings that they have. 
This Bill, under section 3, cons titutes an Advocates' Welfare Fund. 
There are enabling clauses as to fr om where monies can come in. The 
Governments can also make contributions to the Fund.

[22 August. 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
The Bar Councils, the Bar Associations, can make contributions to 
the Funds, but the principal distinction between this and the State Funds is -- 
we have studied the experience of all the States -- we had written to all the 
States to share those experiences with us -- I also had a occasion to discuss it 
with the cross-section of the la wyer community an d their elected 
representatives — one of the problems that we noted was — that membership 
in a large number of State Funds was no t compulsory, and, therefore, when it 
was made optional, the optional memb ership experience did not succeed in 
some States. It succeeded where the me mbership was compulsory. So. -there 
is a compulsory membership; there is an  entry fee into the Fund; there is an 
annual renewal fee. The principal source of funding, in addition to this, comes 
from two sources. Twenty per cent of what the Bar Councils collect, by way 
of enrolment fee from lawyers, will be transferred to this Fund. And, 
additionally, every lawyer -- it has been made clear in this Bill -- out of his 
own earning, and not by transferring the burden to his clients, is expected to 
put a welfare stamp on the wakalatnama of every case he files. Now, this 
welfare stamp, for subordinate courts, has been fixed at five rupees; for 
tribunals, other authorities, High Courts, Supreme Courts, it has been kept at 
ten rupees. So, there are two sides in a case, the amount will get doubled 
because both will have to put that welfare stamp. This Welfare Fund would 
be managed and administered by a committee which is constituted in every 
State. The Committee would be headed by the Advocate General of .the State. 
It will have the Chairman of the Bar Council, Secretary of the Bar Council, 
the Law Secretary of the State Govern ment and also some members of the 
Bar Council. It is this Committee which will administer this Fund. The sale of 
these stamps will also be administered  by this Committee. There are several 
terms with regard 10 the appointment of members and their disqualifications, 
but section 18 makes the membership of the Fund compulsory for all 
advocates. 
With regard to the benefits that the advocates would get out of this 
Fund, there are three different provisions. Section 19, section 21 and section 
24. Section 19 provides for a Trust, giving an ex-gratia payment to any 
member of the Fund, in the event of his serious illness or surgery -- they will 
take into consideration all circumstances; what his other financial 
circumstances are. Section 21 has a Schedule attached to the Bill, that on 
cessation of practice, a token amount w ill be given to every advocate. The 
third and the most important section is section 24 which provides for different 
kinds of assistances which can be given,  like obtaining group

insurances, life insurances, medical and educational facilities, for young 
lawyers, some assistance in terms of books. And there are other provisions 
which can be made, in the event of his d. th. Whatever scheme the State 
Committee, the Trust Committee, would fo n.jlate, his family members would 
get that assistance, in the event of his death, and this amount will actually be a 
substantial amount. In the even of his death, it will be the social security 
amount which is given to his family. There is also a provision, that because 
amenities in various courts are still lacking, 10 per cent of what is collected 
will be spent on common amenities, as far as the district and the subordinate 
Bar Associations are concerned, because that is where the amenities are 
required to be improved upon. 
There are two other provisions. One, some of the benefits of this 
Fund may not be available to those who are designated senior advocates 
because it is presumed that they have a larger practice, and, therefore, may 
not need the benefits of this Fund  -- they are only entitled to certain 
collective group benefits out of this Fund. There is also a provision that as 
far as the Schedules attached to this  Fund are concerned, if some States 
have a larger amount available with them, they can always amend and 
improve upon those Schedules, in the cont ext of those States. There is also 
an appeal provision; if somebody is dissatisfied with any decision of the 
Trust which has been created, an appeal  lies to the full Bar Council of that 
particular State. Theref ore, the overall scheme, as far as this Bill is 
concerned, appears to be that, substantially, the funds for this will come 
from the legal community themselves, unless somebody voluntarily gives to 
them. These funds would be administered and improved upon by depositing 
them or by group insurance, etc. There would be a Committee comprising 
of their own elected representatives, w ith the Advocate Gene ral as the head, 
which would provide the social secur ity mechanism. Now, I must mention 
that 16 States -- this is specified in Schedule II -- have already legislated. 
We have included a saving clause in re spect of all these State legislations 
because the subject is in the Concu rrent List. Unless, on account of 
compulsory membership and certain othe r salient features, some States feel 
that it is beneficial to come within the scope of the Central legislation, then
  
we have the power to delete that particular State out of Schedule II, and they 
would also be entitled to the benefits of the Central legislation. Madam, I 
propose that this House takes this up for consideration and approval. 
The question was proposed.

SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Thank you, 
Madam. I rise to support the Advocates ' Welfare Fund Bill , 2001. The object 
of the Bill, that is, to provide social security to advocates, is laudable. The 
advocates play a vital rote in protecting the rights of the citizens and also in 
upholding the rule of law. Madam, the role played by the lawyers during the 
freedom struggle is commendable; ther efore, any move to create a welfare 
fund for the lawyers must be supported. Sir, while supporting the Bill, I would 
like to point out one or two things. The Bill proposes to bring about 
uniformity in the operation of Advocates' Welfare Fund in various States. But 
Madam, the purpose of the Bill is virtually watered down by the saving 
clause. As per this clause, this Act will not apply to the 16 States which have 
their own laws, as specified in Schedule II. Therefore, there is a possibility of 
these 16 States not adopting this Bill when it becomes an Act. Sir, it will be 
better if, in a matter like this, there is some uniformity throughout the country. 
Now, Madam, I would like to point out the second anomaly. The 
Bill provides that whenever the Committee is superseded, the funds are 
220 

[22 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
transferred to the appropriate Governme nt. There is also a provision in the 
Bill that the Committee has to be re-constituted within a period of six 
months. If that is the case, why sh ould the funds be transferred to the 
Government? I feel, it is wholly unnecessary, and this can be deleted. 
Sir, the other thing that I would like to suggest, which I feel is very, 
very important, is that the interest of the young advocates, the advocates who 
enrol themselves, has to be protected. Ju st as we are taking care of advocates 
who have given up practice, who are old in age. similarly, the young lawyers 
need to be supported. Madam, it is at th at time they require a lot of support, 
as they go through a lot of priva tions and difficulties. Therefore, my 
suggestion is that some amount must be earmarked for the welfare of the 
young advocates, particular ly, for enabling them to set up libraries, because 
library is a tool for any advocate. Some portion of the financial assistance 
must be earmarked for this purpose. 
Madam, another important thing, I feel, is that there should not be 
any fetters on the Committee as to who should be given the benefits and who 
should not, because the Committee is headed by the Advocate-General, and 
competent Advocates are there on the Co mmittee. Therefore, it must be left 
to the discretion of the Committee to decide as to who should get the benefit. 
The best beneficiaries should be thos e who need the fund the most.  I am 
borrowing the words of the hon. Minister. 
Madam, the last point that I would like to make is that it would have 
been ideal had the Central Government given some corpus to the Advocates' 
Welfare Fund. Their concern for the we lfare of the advocates would have 
been better appreciated had they contributed some amount to it. I understand, 
some States are doing this. If the Central Government also thinks on those 
lines, it would be better, but, anyway, there is a provision which says that the 
Central and State Governments can contribute money to this welfare fund. 
With these words. Madam, I support the Bill. Thank you. 
SHRI KA. RA. SUBBIAN (Tamil Nadu): Thank you, Madam Deputy 
Chairman. I wholeheartedly welcome this Bill. I appreciate the hon. Minister 
for having brought forward this enactment. Since our hon. Minister was a 
leading lawyer, he thought it fit to bring this Advocates' Welfare Fund Bill. 
The intention of the hon. Minister has to be appreciated, because the Bill has 
been brought with the good intention of helping the indigent and disabled 
lawyers, taking into consideration the plight and pitiable condition 
221 

RAJYA SABHA [22 August. 2001] 
of these lawyers. I would like to reques t to the Minister to incorporate the 
meaning of 'Senior Advocates' in th e definition clause. As far as the 
advocates in the High Courts and the Supreme Court are concerned, they are 
enlisted as senior advocates on the basis of their standing in the Bar. But, in 
the case of the advocates in the distri ct and mofussil courts, they are not 
classified as such. Theref ore, I would request the hon. Minister that in the 
Definition Clause, he should incorporate the senior advocates as those who 
have put in 20 years to 25 years of standing as lawyers. 
Regarding the amount constituting the Welfare Fund, there are 
several categories specified under Sectio n 3, sub-clause 1, sub-clause 2 and 
sub-clause 8. There it is said that the grant may be made by the Central 
Government or a State Government to the fund after the appropriation is 
made in this regard. Our leader, Dr. Anna mentioned in this august body, 
when he was a Member of the Rajya Sabha , that 'may' is not a forceful word. 
So, my request is that the word 'may' should be substituted by 'shall', to make 
it a mandatory provision. 
That apart, my request is that the words, "to include the fund in the 
corpus, the Central Government or a State Government" should be deleted. 
Instead there should be a mandatory provision so that the Central Government 
as well as the State Government shou ld contribute towards the Advocates' 
Welfare Fund. 
As far as the constitution of the Advocates' Welfare Fund Trustee 
Committee is concerned, the participation of the lawyers should be made 
more liberal. At present only two advo cates are nominated by the State Bar 
Council. Since this Act is for the welfar e of the lawyers, their participation in 
number should be greater. 
Finally, as far as my State is concerned, this scheme was introduced 
there as early as 1986 and an amendment to it was made in the year 1995. On 
the death of an advocate, a sum of Rs.1/- lakh was paid to the legal heirs. On 
his cessation of practice, the advocate wa s paid Rs.50,000/-. When our great 
leader, Dr. Kalaignar, was the Chief Mini ster of the State, he brought in an 
amendment in the year 2,0 00 to the effect that on the death of a lawyer, his 
family and his legal heir are entitled to  Rs.2/-lakhs while on the cessation of 
practice of a lawyer, he is elegible to get Rs.1/- lakh. 
Since 16 States have already adop ted this welfare fund measure and 
you are passing it to be made applicable to all the States uniformly,

keeping in view the prevailing cost of living, I would request that the Central 
and State Governments should contribute to the Fund and that a uniform code 
should be there, whereby on the death of a lawyer, the heir of the deceased 
should get Rs.5/- lakhs and on the cessa tion of practice of an advocate, he 
should get at least Rs.2.5 lakhs. The welfare measures should be made 
applicable uniformly, irrespective of the fact whether the advocate is senior

SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN (Ke rala): Thank you, Madam 
Deputy Chairperson, for giving me an opportunity to speak on the Advocates' 
Welfare Fund Bill, 2001. 
Madam, the legal profession is bein g considered as one of the noble 
professions in the world. This Bill is ai med as a welfare legislation as far as 
the advocate community or the legal fraternity is concerned. So, I support the 
Bill, in principle. But the contents of the Bill are totally disappointing. In the 
year 1980, the Kerala Legislative Assembly had passed a similar Bill, 
namely, the Advocates' Welfare Fund Bill; and that is in force since 1980. It 
is now 21 years old. As per that Act, the amount that used to be given to an 
advocate after 30 years of practice was Rs. 1 lakh. Now, it has been enhanced 
to Rs. 3 lakhs. The same Bill or the same Act is there. Here, as per this new 
legislation, an advocate is getting Rs. 30,000 after 30 years of practice. The 
admission fee is Rs. 200, the annual subscription is Rs. 50, and the 
vakalatnama welfare stamp fee is Rs. 5. So, an advocate or a practitioner who 
is contributing such an amount to the fund, after 30 years of practice would 
get a meagre amount of Rs. 30,000. That is why I have said that this Bill is 
totally disappointing, and this cannot be considered a welfare legislation. 
Madam, considering that an advocate is giving Rs. 50 as annual subscription, 
and, let us say, he is filing not less than 1000 vakalatnamas in a year, one can 
imagine how much amount he is contributing in a particular year. And he is 
getting back this amount after three decades, after 30 years. What would be 
the value of money after 30 years? Is it a profit or loss? What is the benefit 
available to the advocates after 30 years? My humble submission is that 
taking into consideration the other welfare measures, which are there in other 
States, this Bill has to be modified in future, but, for the time being, this 
could be accepted in principle, as far as a welfare legislation for the advocates 
is concerned. 
Madam, the advocate's life is in three stages. We know junior 
advocate's situation is no good. In Malayaiam there is a proverb, which says:  
the first stage he has  no case and no fees.   In the second stage,

is nothing of his going to the court. 
Sir, about the LLB course, legally I would like to highlight a point to

SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. 
Vice-Chairman, Sir, I thank you for giving me an opportunity to participate in 
the discussion on the failure of the public distribution system and the need for 
revamping it. Sir, I think, this issue is of serious concern to one and all, 
irrespective of political affiliations. Therefore, I feel, this issue should be kept 
above politics. This is my humble submission. 
Sir, two days back, the Supreme Court had expressed a serious 
concern over the starvation deaths in some States and observed, "It is the 
primary responsibility of the Central Government and State Governments to 
ensure the foodgrains overflowing in the FCI godowns reach ed the starving 
people and not wasted by dumping them in the sea or eaten by rats." It has 
further observed, "Even if the foodgrains had to be given free, it should be 
done as no person should be deprived  of food, merely because he had no 
money." Even the Planning Commission, in its mid-term appraisal of the 
Ninth Five-Year Plan has mentioned, "All is not well with the PDS." The 
subsidy earmarked for the PDS in 1997-98 was of Rs.7,500 crores. Now it 
has gone up to Rs. 12.042 crores. Much  of this subsidy is not reaching the 
families living below the poverty line for whom it is earmarked. 
Sir, in response to several complaints and recommendations of the 
Standing Committee, a study was conducted by the Tata Economic 
Consultancy Services. It was found that 36 per cent of wheat, 31 per cent of 
rice, and 23 per cent of sugar was diverted. The diversion is more in the 
Northern States, Eastern States and in the North-Eastern Region. I am quoting 
this from the mid-term appraisal document. It is comparatively less in the  
Southern and Western regions. 
A high 64 per cent diversion of rice is estimated in Bihar and Assam. 
The hon. Minister, while replying to the debate on the FCI Bill, stated that a 
quantity of 303 lakh tonnes has been allotted to the States and UTs, but they 
have lifted only 130 lakh tonnes. Even at the ration shop level, the offtake is less. 
The reasons for the poor offtake at the ration shop level can be only two. One is 
the lack of purchasing power and the other is the bad quality of foodgrains.

some of the problems associated with the scheme are -

that half of the Food Corporation's grains stocks is at least two years

hurdles, if any, being faced in the implementation and find a methodology for

programme. I appeal to the political and social workers at the village level to

a problem has been created that way. The offtake, over the last few years, has 
been declining. Many speakers, even you, Sir, and many before me, have said 
that the offtake has been low, and they  have enumerated the reasons why the 
offtake has been low, but I will not go into that. I would only state a few 
other things. 
Apart from hiking up the subsidy bill of the Government due to 
storage and interest costs of holding excess stocks of foodgrains, the excess 
stocks can also bring problems from India's international commitments. Sir, 
you know WTO. WTO allows a public distribution system only for the 
purpose of food security- holding stocks in excess of what is considered 
necessary for food security will be co nsidered as a subsidy given to the 
producers. If you hold too much of foodgrains in your godowns, WTO will 
definitely pull us up, and the Government will have to pay for that; they will 
have to answer for that. Holding of large-scale foodgrains in godowns is not 
allowed in the WTO and that might invite retaliatory actions from other 
member-countries. Problems from WTO might also arise if the Government 
continues with its attempt of exporting wheat at a subsidised price for too 
long. Both these problems, if they arise, are completely avoidable, which will 
put India into a problem at the international front with no benefit to the 
population. So, we should be very, very cautious of that. 
Then, again, we have been saying that we have got plenty of food. 
But, Sir, if you see the statistics, if yo u see the graph, we will realise that the 
foodgrain production stood at minus 4.7 per cent for the last financial year. It 
has been consistently growing below the rate of growth of population for 
quite some time now. Such a phenomenon (where the rate of growth of 
foodgrain production falls short of the rate of growth of population) is often 
referred to as 'Malthusian Trap of Hunger', and has reappeared for the first 
time since it was removed after independence. We cannot afford to be 
complacent. We cannot say that we have  got a problem of plenty but we are 
producing less, and our problem is going up. So, we have to apply our mind 
to these problems, Sir. 
The two mismatched sides of the picture will seem even more ironic 
if we consider the fact that India ha s one of the most well developed public 
distribution systems in the world. In spite of that, we are having these 
problems.

Ironically, the mess that the food sector of the country is in right 
now, is completely created by the present Government, through its policies 
during the last few years. What are t hose policies? The policies are what we 
are doing. How is the management of the Public Distribution System done? It 
is done by procurement and distribution. Even a small chaiwala. or a 
subziwala buys, and he sells, and in the bargain, he makes money. And here, 
we have bungled! 
The procurement prices have been  steadily increasing in the recent 
times and have consistently stayed above the levels recommended by the 
Committee of Agricultural Procurement.  Given this, the procurement has 
steadily been increasing in the recent times. 
The direct reason for increase in procurement prices is an increase in 
pressures from political parties from some of the agricultural States. 
However, a more important reason, again, lies in the policies and actions of 
the Government in the recent times, which has resulted in a steady increase in 
the cost of inputs for agriculture. 
For instance, there is a decline in subsidy. There is a decline in 
public expenditure in agriculture. The farmers have to spend themselves. 
There is the Exim Policy. There is th e WTO because of which people had to 
go in for cash crops. Now, the cash crops have suffered. They are again going 
in for wheat and rice. All these things  are affecting our food distribution 
system. Given the conditions, a steadily increasing procurement price has 
become a necessity for the survival of  the farmers. The farmers cannot grow 
anything else. So, they have to grow these commodities and they know that

In the case of distribution also, the position is the same. We have

pronounced on the floor of the Parliament by an opposition Member --the 
diktat was "Thou shalt have to reduce subsidies on the food items of mass 
consumption, even if it is painful." I add, even if it leads to starvation deaths 
of the common people of the country. I am sorry to make my observation that 
the people who held power in this country in hitherto Governments hardly 
cared for the poor, the ma rginalised, ill-fated, people. For them, only some 
lip-service and electoral assurances we re considered to be sufficient. 
However, let me come back to one of th e most bizarre features of the present 
PDS, virtually, we are discussing a post-facto situation, making a post-facto 
analysis of the present system. It is quite intriguing that contrary to the 
predicament, as I have already stated , suddenly, the food subsidy has been 
increased by almost 50'per cent. But has the PDS distributed 50 per cent more 
grains? No. I want to say that the foodgrain offtake from PDS has 
plummeted. In 1999-2000, the offtake of wheat was less than half the 
allocation. In the first nine months of 2000-2001, the offtake was a little over 
one-third of the allocation. In the case of rice, in 1999-2000, the offtake was 
4/5th of the allocation. In the first nine months of 2000-2001. The offtake fell 
to a little over half the allocation. During 1998-2001 there was a boom in the 
procurement of both rice and wheat. So , the procurement continued and the 
offtake plummetted. It is a paradoxical situation. The foodgrains stock rose to 
a staggering proportion, much above the buffer stock norms. Thereby a 
disastrous situation arose. I want to give some instances as to how the issue 
prices of wheat and rice under the PDS have gone up. Let me quote some 
figures, the rate per

quintal. In 1999-2000, the rate of the so-called BPL wheat, per quintal was 
Rs.250, whereas in 2000-2001, it is Rs.415, a rise of 66 per cent. In the APL 
cases, in 1999-2000, it was Rs.682; and in 2000-2001, it is Rs.830, a 
stagerring rise of 21.7 per cent. In the case of rice, it is from Rs.352 to 
Rs.565, that is, a 61.4 per cent rise in  the issue price; and from Rs.905 to 
Rs.1130, that is, a 24.9 per cent rise in the issue price. Whom have we 
benefited? Let us understand that. The reason for that is, perhaps, known to 
all. and that is, the steep rise in the issue prices of foodgrains under the Public 
Distribution System has cut the pff-take, leading to huge idle stocks and 
higher operating costs. The so-called APL consumers have been virtually 
evicted from the arena of the PDS by pricing foodgrains at the FCI's so-called 
'economic cost' which is near the market price in most of India and even 
higher in some places of the country. The hon. Mini ster of Food and Civil 
Supplies must note this. Naturally, the APL consumers had to opt out of the 
PDS en masse. That leaves only the BPL cons umers, the below poverty line 
consumers, who are to receive grains at fifty per cent of the economic cost. In 
many States, the Governments have managed to whittle down the number of 
BPL consumers to a fraction of the official poverty estimates. 
The 2000-01 Budget announced that  the allocation per BPL family 
had been increased from 10 kg. a month to 20 kg. If the entire BPL allocation 
had been drawn in the course of the year, the off-take would have been 14.3 
million tonnes, which would have required a subsidy of Rs.7500 crores. 
However, it appeared that in fact, even  the BPL allocation had not been fully 
drawn, since, during the first nine months of the year, less than 8.5 million 
tonnes were drawn. On an extended calculation for 12 months, it could be at 
best it.3 million tonnes. Of this, the subsidy would be around Rs.6000 crores, 
even assuming that virtually all the off-take is BPL. As against less than 
Rs.6000 crores of actual subsidy, the food subsidy was Rs. 12,215 crores. 
That is, more than half the so-called food subsidy was spent as carrying cost 
of the swelling foodgrains stock. Unfortunately, neither the survey nor the 
Budget gives any break-up of the cost between the carrying cost of stocks and 
other costs. 
To reduce this burgeoning foodstocks, the Government of India is 
exporting foodgrains. I am sorry that the international prices of rice and wheat 
are far below our domestic price, since the advanced developed countries 
heavily subsidise the farmers. I just qu ote an instance. The United States of 
America paid its six million farmers a staggering amount of 
286 

[22 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
167 billion dollars in 1995-96. So, the Government of India is exporting 
Indian wheat at the price at which it sells it to the BPL consumers. The 
remaining portion, that is fifty per cent of the FCPs so-called 'economic cost', 
is subsidised by the Government and the Government would be spending 
Rs.415 crores--a staggering amount-on each million tonne of wheat exported. 
So is the case with rice. The Government, loath to provide any subsidy to its 
own citizens' consumption, is happy to subsidise export! 
Sir, I must mention this. The height of absurdity has been attained by 
the Antyodaya Anna Yojana launched in  the month of December, 2000, by 
the hon. Prime Minister, on his birth day, no less in true feudal style. This 
scheme is purportedly intended to provide 25 kg. of foodgrains per family per 
month, at a special rate of Rs.2 per kg. for wheat and Rs.3 per kg, for rice. 
However, this is to go only to the poorest of the poor, to 10 million families, 
that is, one-fifth of the Government's so-called estimate or underestimation of 
the poor. How will these lucky 10 million be found out? Have we initiated 
some survey to find out these 10 mill ion families who are the poorest of the 
poor? By what norms will you be dete rmining that? The estimated annual 
allocation of foodgrains for the scheme would be three million tonnes. A 
subsidy of Rs.2315 crores is announced by you. This ridiculous scheme 
shows the direction in which the PDS is heading, virtual winding up, with 
only a few demonstrative crumbs and arbitrarily selected poor families. Sir, it 
is difficult to "avoid the conclusion. Sir, it is difficult to avoid the conclusion 
that the problem of excess foodgrains stocks has been deliberately allowed to 
grow to the crisis proportion in order to strengthen the argument that there is 
no shortage of foodgrains, and so, th ere is no reason that the Public 
Distribution System should continue; secondly, the burden of the procurement 
is too great for the Government to bear and so, it must be left to the private 
traders, the multinational corporations and other companies, and you will be 
finding out your own solace and own logic of divesting the entire property to 
the private traders, the big multinationals or the big Indian companies. That is 
why despite Rs. 4,115 crores overrun in the food subsidies, the World Bank 
and the pro-establishment media have not cared to criticise the gross waste. It 
serves their long term purpose, and Sir, I must say that it is high time for all of 
us, not only the Parliamentarians, but also the good citizens of this country, 
that they must ponder over this very serious situation, where the Government 
has become a party to conspire against the poorest of the poor population of 
this country. It is a conspiracy which has been unmasked, it is a policy 
framework which has been intended to conspire against the common people, 
the poor people of

our time, and we cannot afford to waste our time. With these words, I 
conclude. Thank you very much.

SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE: Sir, I would not put these two together. I 
would not say the sickness in industry is because of globalisation. But I would say here 
that the information on sickness is not maintained centrally, neither State-wise. The 
information comes to us from the RBI and it is true that in the last year the figure of 
sickness was 3,04,000. Apart from the composite package, we have taken other measures 
to deal with the sickness. The State-level Institutional Committees have been set up for 
timely identification and rehabilitation of the potentially viable sick industries. Special 
Rehabilitation Cells in banks and other State financial institutions have been set up 
and elaborate guidelines have been issued by the RBI for extending rehabilitation 
assistance to eligible units. A one-time settlement formula, the Samadhan Scheme, 
has been announced by the RBI on 27th July, 2000 for the settlement of dues. There is a 
Delayed Payment Act which provides for penal interest on delayed payments to small 
units. This has also been helpful in reducing some sickness due to delayed payments. 
Finally, as per our comprehensive policy package, we have set up a Committee to 
draw up revised guidelines for the rehabilitation of me currently sick but potentially 
viable SSI units. The RBI has already received the report of the Committee. The RBI is 
drawing up fresh guidelines. We are waiting for intimation from the RBI. I am sure it 
will help us in the early detection of sick units and timely revival of sick industries.

Activities conducted by NCP 
*443. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state:  
(a) what are the main aims and obj ectives of National Commission on 
Population (NCP); 
(b) the activities conducted by NCP since January, 2001; 
(c) the funds allocated for the NCP during the current year; and 
(d) the achievements of NCP since its inception? 
15 

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2001 ] 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. CR 
THAKUR): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The main aims and objectives of the National Commission on 
Population are given below: 
(1) To review, monitor and give directions for the implementation of the 
National Population Policy with a view to meeting the goals set out 
in the policy. 
(2) To promote synergy between demographic, educational, 
environmental and developmental programmes so as to hasten 
population stabilization. 
(3) To promote inter-sectoral coordination in planning and 
implementation across government agencies of the Central and State 
Governments, to involve the civil society and the private sector and 
to explore the possibilities of international cooperation in support of 
the goals set out in the Policy. 
(4) To facilitate the development of a vigorous people's movement in 
support of this national effort. 
(b) and (d) Brief details of the activities/achievements of the NCP are given 
below: 
1. Review of the implementation of National Family Welfare Programme 
TJie present growth in the population of the country is basically due to 
three factors. About 60% of  the growth can be attributed to the large size of 
the population in the repr oductive age group.  This is bound to take place 
because of what has happened in the past. Another 20% of the growth in 
population is said to be due to the high unmet needs fo r contraception. The 
balance 20% is due to other socio-economic factors like high infant mortality, 
low status of women, son preference, illiteracy, poverty, etc. 
The elements of population growth amenable to policy intervention 
relate to the latter two categories, namely meeting the unmet needs for 
contraception and improving the social , economic and demographic factors 
affecting population growth. The National Population Policy (NPP) 2000 states 
that the unmet needs for basic reproductive and child health services, supplies 
and infrastructure should be met at the earliest. If the unmet needs for 
16 

[23 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
contraceptives can be met, especially in the high population growth States like Uttar 
Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh, the same could go a long way in 
reducing the overall population growth significantly. In view of the crucial role of these 
States in achieving the objectives of demographic stabilization, Vice-Chairman, 
NCP took two meetings with the Chief Secretaries/Family Welfare Secretaries of 
these States for a thorough review of the implementation of the Family Welfare 
Programmes. These reviews have helped to identify the various problems in each State 
and the remedial measures required. Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and UP have since 
brought out their separate population policy documents along with a programme of 
action for population stabilization within a time frame. Bihar is in the process of finalizing 
its population policy. The Member Secretary, NCP has also visited UP, Madhya Pradesh 
and Bihar to discuss the issues relating to population stabilization with concerned 
State Government officials. 
At the national level, the implementation of the Family Welfare 
Programmes was reviewed in a meeting taken by Vice-Chairman, NCP with Minister 
for Health and Family Welfare on 9.8.2001, in which the present level of use of 
different types of contraceptives, the couple protection rate, the financial and 
physical achievements etc. were examined and the need for a restrategisation of the 
programme was brought out. The need for drawing up area specific action plans to 
improve social, economic and demographic factors in the high fertility areas was 
emphasized. The necessity for evolving a mechanism for involving the Panchayati 
Raj Institutions, NGOs, women self-help groups and promoting public and private 
participation was brought out in order to ensure that the services reached the 
needy. 
2. Identification of high fertility districts and preparation of District Action 
Plans 
There are considerable inter-State and intra-State differences relating to 
demographic indicators. The district being the key unit in implementing various 
programmes, the NCP has undertaken an exercise to identify the high fertility 
districts in the country. This has shown that there are 133 districts having above 
3.5 Total Fertility Rate (TFR) and another 196 districts with TFR between 2.5 and 
3.5 against the NPP target of reaching replacement level TFR of 2.1 by 2010 for the 
country as a whole. After this, as a first step, the Commission convened a meeting of 
the District Magistrates of the 133 high fertility districts to understand the ground 
realities as also to sensitise them about the various issues which have a bearing on 
populatior 
17 

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2001] 
growth. After detailed discussions, the District Magistrates resolved to bring up 
population related issues upfront which involve fully meeting the unmet needs for 
reproductive and child health services so as to reach the replacement level fertility at 
the earliest. They further decided that District Action Plans would be prepared 
with short-term, medium-term and l ong-term objectives. The action plans 
prepared/being prepared will bring out the position about the infrastructure, 
human and other resources available and the existing gaps in them with a definite 
programme of action for covering these gaps within a given time frame. 
3. Selection of social, economic and demographic indicators for 
monitoring purpose 
The NCP document is noteworthy in that it transcends purely 
demographic concerns and aims at the over-riding objective of economic and 
social development to improve the quality of life of the people of India. In this 
perspective, it was also felt that the traditional ways of monitoring the progress 
in terms of financial and physical achievements might not serve the purpose in 
identifying factors leading to high population growth. Therefore, after extensive 
discussions, the NCP selected some social, economic and demographic indicators 
such as female literacy, age of marriage of girls, safe delivery for mother, child 
survival, clean drinking water supply, basic sanitation facility, child nutrition, 
immunization and adoption of family planning methods which directly or 
indirectly influence human fertility. In the light of the deliberations at the DM's 
Conference, the list of indicators were modified. Then, using the data from Census 
2001 and other sources, the NCP has ranked and mapped 569 districts of the 
country on the basis of 12 social, economic and demographic indicators and a 
composite index based on them with a view to know the comparative position of 
each district in relation to these indicators. This data was published on the occasion 
of World Population Day on 11 th July, 2001. The information/data brought out by 
this publication is useful to policy-makers, administrators, researchers and all those 
who are concerned with regional di sparities in economic and social 
development. The regular collection, analysis and publication of data relating to 
these indicators will be a major change in the strategy for monitoring the 
implementation of social sector programmes. For this purpose, a Standing 
Committee for Monitoring of the NCP has been set up with representatives of the 
concerned Central Ministries, State Governments and NGOs as recommended by the 
Task Force on Monitoring chaired by the Vice-Chairman, NCP. 
18 

[23 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
4. Conference of Demographic Research Organisations 
As envisaged in the,NPP, integration of  the results of research with policy 
formulation is important for effectively addressing various issues related to 
population stabilization. Therefore, on 20th March, 2001, the NCP convened a 
Conference of the organizations/experts involved in demographic research: This 
Conference was attended by representa tives of 19 Population Resarch Centres 
(PRCs) from all over India, Indian Institute of Management, Lucknow, Indian 
Council for Medical Research, Institute for Economic Growth, New Delhi, United 
Nations Fund for Population - Activities (UNFPA), UNICEF, noted demographers, 
NGOs and senior officers from the concerned Departments of the Government of 
India. The NCP plans to utilize the PRCs and other research organizations in 
evaluation studies of social sector programmes. Such studies have already been 
sponsored by the Commission in relation to Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. 
The proper utilization of the results of the research and evaluation studies can help 
improve the quality, reduce the cost and introduce the required changes from time 
to time in policies and programmes. 
5. The recommendations of the Working Groups constituted by the NCP 
On the basis of decisions taken at the Strategic Support Group of Secretaries 
of the concerned Departments, the NCP had constituted some Working Groups to 
examine the strategies for meeting the unmet needs for contraception, maternal, child 
and public health, empowerment of women, development of children, drinking water, 
nutrition, sanitation, issues relating to adolescents, main streaming of the Indian 
system of medicine, tribal communities, monitoring and media for information, 
education and communication. Most of these Groups have already completed their work 
and submitted their recommendations/reports. These are being integrated to the extent 
possible in the policies and programees for the 10th Five Year Plan. The programme of 
action emerging out of these recommendations will also be considered in separate 
meetings with each of the concerned Ministries at the Centre and the States. 
6. Evolving grass-root level models 
The NPP document mentions that Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) are important 
for furthering decentralized planning and programme implementation. It also states 
that population stabilization efforts will be effective only if an integrated package of 
essential services are reached at the village 
19 

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2001] 
and household levels. Presently, many of the services and programmes of social 
sectors are not reaching the people at th e village level in the desired manner. 
There is also a multiplicit y of agencies and employ ees representing different 
departments working in the rural areas in an uncoordinated manner. Because of 
uiis, there is a need to think about alternative for ensuring better delivery of 
services and supplies at the village level and for maintenance of the infrastructure 
facilities in sectors like health, family welfare and education. For this purpose, 
the active involvement of elected representatives of PRIs, NGOs and village 
self-help groups active at the grass-root level is important. In an effort to develop 
appropriate models/strategies and to understand innovative policies and 
programmes being implemented in some places, the NCP has organized field 
visits to some of the village Panchayats in high fertility areas. Some members of 
the Commission and representatives of the national level NGOs also participated 
in these visits, which may help evolve alternative strategies for meeting the 
unmet needs relating to different social sectors in the rural areas. Points for 
action which emerged out of these visits include control and supervision of all 
village level functionaries by PRIs, training programmes for women members 
of PRIs, self-help groups, etc. to improve their awareness and empowerment, 
involving the practitioners of Indian System of Medicine and Homeopathy to 
fill the gaps in human resources, coordinating the functioning of all social 
sector field level workers and adoption of contract system of employment with 
performance related incentives for field level employees. The involvement of 
PRIs and village level organizations can help preparation of Panchayat Action 
Plans to address specific issues rela ting to population stabilization in each 
Panchayat/village. To help operationalise the District Action Plans, the Panchayat 
Action Plans are also being encouraged.

*444. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the

(a) Whether the thermometers used for measuring body temperature now

thermometers find dieir way to me chemist shops across die country; and

manufacturers get ISI standardisation mark on die product tfiey put for sale in the

THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHANTA KUMAR): (a) There have been reports that 
some of the clinical thermometers available in the market are inaccurate and/or 
deficient in certain other aspects. 
(b) The Standards of Weights & Measures Act 1976 provides that 
24 

[23 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
every unit of weight or measures shall be based on the metric system. 
Thermometers are, therefore, to be marked only in degree Celsius. Most of the 
manufacturers, however, have been making thermometers with Fahrenheit 
marking or dual marking, i.e. with degree Fahrenheit and Celsius. Manufacture, 
sale and use of such non-standard thermometers amounts to contravention of the 
Standards of Weights & Measures Act, 1976 and the Standards of Weights & 
Measures (Enforcement) Act, 1985. Such non-standard thermometers are, 
therefore, not submitted by the manufacturers for verification by the Weights & 
Measures enforcement authorities in the States. Enforcement authorities in some 
States are carrying out inspections of retail shops to check the sale of non-standard 
thermometers and launching prosecution in suitable cases. 
(c) Government propose to take action under the Bureau of Indian Standards 
(BIS) Act, 1986 to direct the use of the BIS standard mark under a license as 
compulsory for enclosed scale and solid stem type clinical thermometers to 
ensure that such thermometers manufactured and sold in the market meet the 
requirements of the Weights & Measures laws and also conform to the quality 
standards prescribed by BIS.

Job Opportunities for Industrial Labour 
*449. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the causes of the present slump in job market for industrial labour in the 
country; 
(b) the details of the measures taken by Government, recently, in regard to 
improvements in job opportunities for industrial labour; 
(c) whether Government have taken note of the recommendations of the 
Montek Singh Committee in this regard; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) the measures taken by Government to implement the 
recommendations and ease slump in job market and eliminate present 
sufferings of the industrial labour? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (DR. SATYA NARAYAN JATIYA): (a) to (e) 
The main reasons for not achieving the desired growth rate of employment for 
industrial labour in the country are as follows: 
1. Present rate of economic growth not being in tune with the 
requirements for employment generation. 
2. Employment opportunities in the old industries are getting reduced due to 
closer of older type of enterprises. 
29 

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2001] 
3. Old technologies are getting replaced by new technologies, the 
demand for unskilled and semi-skilled workers are less. Skilled 
labour are more in demand in these new industries. 
4. In the present scenario, the employment rate has come down since the 
average skill level of the workers is not in tune with demand of the 
labour market. 
In order to cope up with the situation indicated above, Government is 
revising the courses run by Industrial Training Institutes. At the same time, new 
trades are being introduced as per the demand of the market. Same procedure is 
followed for Apprenticeship Training Programmes. The Advanced Training 
Institutes under Ministry of Labour is running courses for upgradation of the 
skill level of the workers already employed. 
The report of the Task Force under the Chairmanship of Dr. Montek Singh 
Ahluwalia has been received. The sports suggested generation of employment 
through intervention in 5 major areas as follows: 
* Accelerating the rate of growth of GDP, with a particular emphasis on 
sectors likely to ensure the spread of income to the low income 
segments of the labour force. 
* Pursuing appropriate sectoral policies in individual sectors which are 
particularly important for employment generation. These sector level 
policies must be broadly consistent with the overall objective of 
accelerating GDP growth. 
* Implementing focused special programmes for creating additional 
employment of enhancing income generation from existing activities 
aimed at helping vulnerable groups that may not be sufficiently 
benefited by the move general growth promoting policies. 
* Pursuing suitable policies for education and skill development, which 
would upgrade the quality of the labour force and make it capable of 
supporting a growth process which geneates high quality jobs. 
The above report is being analysed and further action will be taken as per 
the decision of die Government on it.

inorganic matter, which is a part and parcel of foreign matter like sand, stones, 
pebbles clay particles etc. are not accepted under this category. The explanation 
given by diem was that only organic foreign matter (like chaff, glumes,weed seeds 
and other edible and inedible grains) are taken under this category. The exporters did 
not know tins position. They presumed tiiat, as in the CODEX standards, die 2% 
foreign matter would include upto 0.5% inorganic matter. The delegation was further 
informed uiat die Iraqi flour mills were not having adequate facilities for separation of 
inorganic matter because of die problem of spare parts required for maintenance of 
such machines owing to UN sanctions. The delegation was further informed that Iraq 
had also rejected die wheat sourced from various other countries on die same grounds. 
As die consignment conformed to die CODEX standards, it was accepted in

3368. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: W ill the Minister of CONSUMER

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIRAM 
CHAUHAN): (a) and (b) The State-wise exact quantum of foodgrain losses during 
post harvest period at farm level due to insects, rodents, moisture, birds, micro-
organisms, etc. including State of Punjab, Haryana and Madhya Pradesh is not 
known. However, a Committee headed by Dr. V.G. Panse, in its report submiued in 
1968 had estimated annual post harvest losses in the foodgrains in various stages at 
9.33%. These included losses during threshing 
54 

[23 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(1.68%), transportation (0.15%), processing (0.92%), rodents (2.50%), birds

Reshuffle of Military and Para-Military Force 
3375. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government have undertaken a reorganisation and reshuffle of 
various military, para-military and security forces, including intelligence wings, in 
the context of lesson drawn from the Kargil episode and the possibility of another 
Kargil like situation being presented by Pakistan; and 
(b) if so, the details in this regard indicating the steps taken and being taken 
to avert another Kargil like situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF DEFENCE (SHRI 
KRISHNAMRAJU): (a) and (b) Government had constituted a Group of Ministers 
(GoM) on 17th April, 2000 to thoroughly review the national security system in its 
entirety and, in particular to consider the recomendations of the Kargil Review 
Committee and formulate specific proposals for implementation. The GoM had 
after taking into account the report of the Kargil Review Committee, Reports of the 
four Task Forces set up by the GoM and other inputs, finalised their 
recommendations for reforming the National Security System. The Group of 
Ministers (GoM) has made comprehensive recommendations for strengthening 
the existing processes, procedures and structures related to Defence Management, 
Intelligence Apparatus, Internal Security and Border Management. The 
important recommendations of the GoM relate to (i) redesignation of Service Hqrs as 
"Integrated Headquarters", (ii) creation of the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), (iii) 
creation of a Defence Procurement Board, (iv) the Defence Intelligence Agency, (v) 
the National Defence University, (vi) the preparation of holistic integrated Defence 
Perspective Plans for 15 to 20 years, (vii) strengthening the mechanism for 
gathering and dissemination of intelligence, (viii) rejuvenation of State Police 
Forces/Central Para military Forces, (ix) national service for youth, (x) expanding 
NCC and service in the Territorial Army, (xi) upgradation of the efficacy of the civil 
defence organization, (xii) setting up of village defence committees in rural areas, 
(xiii) revamp of the criminal justice system, (xiv) strengthening, training and 
equipping of Border Guarding Forces etc. The report of the GoM was presented to 
the Prime Minister on 26th February 2001. The Government approved the 
61 

RAJYA SABHA [23 August, 2001 ] 
recommendations made in the Report of the GoM on 11th May, 2001 with the 
modification that a view on the recommendation relating to the institution of the Chief 
of Defence Staff (CDS) will be taken after consultation with various political parties.

order to ensure that the recommendations are implemented in a time bound manner, 
the implementation process is being closely monitored by the Government.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF DEFENCE

(a) to (d) 1. Benefits given by the Government to the families of Kargil 
casualties and disabled soldiers: 
The widows/Next of Kin of the Armed Forces Personnel killed in Kargil 
Operation have been paid an ex-gratia amount of Rs. 10 lakhs each. They have 
been sanctioned liberalized family pension equal to the last pay drawn by the 
deceased personnel and have been granted Death-cum-retirement gratuity as 
admissible under the rules after completion of necessary documentation. 
Soldiers disabled in Kargil Operations and invalided out are entitled to 
War Injury Pension consisting of service element and war injury element as 
under: 
(i) Service Element—equal to retiring/service pension to which the 
individual would have been entitled on the basis of his/her pay on the 
date of invalidment but counting service upto the date on which he/she

earning this element.

100% disablement. However, in no case the aggregate of service element 
and war injury element is to exceed last pay drawn. For lower 
percentage, war injury pension is proportionately reduced. 
On the recommendation of the Medical Board, disabled soldiers are paid 
Constant. Attendance Allowance (CAA) @ Rs. 600/- p.m. for 100% 
disablement. 
Armed Forces Personnel who are retained in service despite disability have 
an option either to (a) draw lump sum compensation in lieu of war injury 
element foregoing war injury elem ent at the time of subsequent 
retirement/discharge or (b) to draw war injury element at the time of retirement in 
addition to retiring/service pension admissible on retirement/discharge.

Government of India are committed to the development of friendly and 
good nieghbourly relations with China on the basis of the principles of 
Panchsheel and mutual sensitivity to each others concerns. This has been 
underscored during recent high level political exchanges between India and China, 
including during the visit of senior Chinese leader and NPC Chairman Mr. Li Peng 
in January 2001 and the visit of Deputy Chairperson of the Rajya Sabha, Smt. 
Najma Heptulla to China in July 2001. 
India and China seek a fair, r easonable and mutually acceptable 
settlement of the boundary question through peaceful consultation. India & China 
have signed an agreement on the Maintenance of Peace and Tranquility along the 
Line of Actual Control in the India-China Border Areas in 1993 and a second 
agreement on Confidence Building Measures in the Military Field along the Line 
of Actual Control in the India-China Border Areas in 1996. These two 
Agreements provide an institutional framework for the maintenance of peace 
and tranquility in the border areas. Both sides have also agreed to expedite the 
process of LAC clarification within existing mechanisms. 
Bilateral trade between India and China has been steadily expanding In the 
year 2000, two-way trade was USS 2.92 billion, an increase of 47%

King; reviewed bilateral relations w ith new Prime Minister Sher Bahadur 
Deuba and exchanged views with top political leaders.
